entries.title: Mother who beat addiction fatally shot snuggling in bed with her 2 daughters, sister and police say
entries.summary: <p>Crystal Salter, inspired by the birth of her daughter, Juliana, spent the last several years of her life helping others climb out of the same drug-fueled position she once found herself in.</p><p>But her life ended abruptly and violently early Sunday.</p><p>That's when, police and relatives say, she was fatally shot by her boyfriend — in front of 7-year-old Juliana and Legacy, the 7-year-old foster daughter she took in this year. </p><p>A couple of hours later, Salter's boyfriend was found dead in his vehicle with a self-inflicted gunshot wound to his mouth, police said. </p><p>"It's unfortunate for her to lose her life to gun violence, for her to lose her life to a person she loved and adored so much," Regina Salter, Crystal Salter's younger sister, said. "It's sad we lost her like this." </p><p>Crystal Salter, 42, was in bed with the two children at her home in the 2100 block of West Jackson Boulevard when she was shot multiple times in her torso and face, police said. She was taken to Stroger Hospital where she was pronounced dead, officials said.</p><p>Juliana, now under her aunt's care, has struggled since her mother's slaying.</p><p>"Can I see my mommy? I want to see my mommy. I want to go home," Juliana will plead, Regina Salter said.</p><p>"I just have to go in one room and cry, or go out on the back porch and cry because there's no love like a mother's love," Regina Salter said. "You can't fill the void of a child's mother."</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-b10000" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crystal Salter “always felt that God gave her a second chance” and that’s all she would talk about, her sister said.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><h3>‘He had a mask on his face’ </h3><p>Crystal Salter met her boyfriend at a South Side gas station last December, and he "worshipped the ground she walked on," Regina Salter said. </p><p>Issues in the relationship, potentially including Crystal Salter taking in Legacy after her mother checked out of a women's treatment center and disappeared, led Salter to give her boyfriend until the end of August to move out of her apartment, according to her sister. </p><p>But Regina Salter never got any inclination that the 49-year-old man, who hasn’t yet been identified by the Cook County medical examiner's office, was capable of such violence. </p><p>"He didn't come off as a person who would fight women or potentially would kill a woman," Regina Salter said. "We were all shocked." </p><p>Five shell casings were found in the bathroom of the apartment, and a large pool of blood was found on a bed, according to a police report obtained by the Chicago Sun-Times. </p><p>In the vehicle where the man was found, officers discovered a Smith & Wesson revolver with four live rounds and a fired shell casing and four additional shell casings on the floorboard of the front passenger area. </p><p>"The first sign that you see from a man, it's time to leave, don't be afraid to reach out to some family or someone close and tell them what's going on," Regina Salter said. "The man that took my sister's life, he wore masks. He had a mask on his face. We didn't know he was like that."</p><h3>Overcoming addiction to help others in a similar situation </h3><p>Crystal Salter was molested and raped in her early 20s, and the trauma led her to become heavily addicted to drugs for roughly a decade, according to her sister. Relatives didn’t know whether they'd lose her to her addiction. </p><p>"We would go see her and go drop her off food and go try and give her money and try to help her get better and get clean, but she didn't," Regina Salter said. "She just wouldn't get help."</p><p>But when she became pregnant with Juliana, Crystal Salter became inspired to get herself off drugs and start a new path forward. </p><p>"It changed Crystal's life for the better, and she got help. She recovered fast, and it made her want to be a voice for others," Regina Salter said. "That's what she's been doing for the last eight years of her life."</p><p>During one trip to Aldi, Crystal Salter saw a woman at a bus stop without shoes and demanded her sister pull over so she could give the woman the shoes off her feet, family recalls. She walked around in socks until she bought a pair of shoes at Aldi. </p><p>"She always felt that God gave her a second chance by giving her Juliana, and that's all she would talk about," Regina Salter said. </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-960000" name="image-960000"></a> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Crystal (left) and Regina Salter had a strong sisterhood. Regina recalls Crystal helping her tie her shoes when they were young, and the sisters — the two youngest of 10 children — grew closer as they got older. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Provided </p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p></p><p>Crystal Salter was never shy about sharing the more turbulent parts of her life with other in hopes of being an inspiration to those in similar circumstances.</p><p>Regina Salter used to advise against her sister sharing certain details about her life, but Crystal Salter stressed it was "her story to tell" and she wanted others to see "there are rainbows after the rain and you can get help and recover."</p><p>Crystal Salter was called a spiritual "beam of joy" involved with her church who also loved barbecue and had dreams of opening a women's shelter to help women and children in need. </p><p>Even after losing her mother to heart failure — her mom never knew she got clean — Crystal Salter stayed devoted to her improved lifestyle. </p><p>"She always was out there helping the community," Regina Salter said. "We were all just so proud of Crystal."</p><h3>Making ends meet to provide stability for a child in need </h3><p>In April, Crystal Salter was driving on the West Side when she spotted a woman she was once in a treatment center with sitting in an alley with her child. </p><p>She offered the woman and 7-year-old girl, Legacy, a place in her apartment before the woman checked herself into a treatment center and left hours later, Regina Salter said. </p><p>After failed attempts to reach Legacy's mother, Crystal Salter gained custody of Legacy days later and used money she saved and the income from work as a call center operator for SCR Transportation, a company that subcontracts to Pace, to provide schooling and stability for Legacy. </p><p>"That kind of position requires patience and kindness while working with vulnerable communities," according to Pace spokesperson Maggie Daly Skogsbakken. </p><p>Said Kristin Persu, a co-worker of Crystal Salter at SCR Transportation: “Crystal was a wonderful team member, and we are deeply saddened to learn of her passing. Our thoughts and prayers are with her family and friends during this difficult time.”</p><p>"She just loved being a mother," Regina Salter said. "So I'm thinking she seen Legacy needed some love, she needed to be in a stable household, she needed to probably get in school because Legacy had been living out on the streets with her mom."</p><div entries.title: Cubs have no animosity toward Brewers, even with another 2nd-place finish looming
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — Hot take: The White Sox-Brewers rivalry in the early days of the American League Central was much hotter than the Cubs-Brewers rivalry of today.</p><p>And those Sox-Brewers games in the mid-1990s never meant anything close to what Cubs-Brewers games have meant for the last decade. The Sox and Brewers never battled each other for first place or even a playoff spot.</p><p>But Sox manager Terry Bevington and Brewers manager Phil Garner, aka “Scrap Iron,” seemed to detest each other. Their feelings boiled over in 1995 when they wrestled in the middle of a benches-clearing brawl that ignited when Sox legend Ozzie Guillen got tangled with Jeff Cirillo after sliding into third base.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> and Brewers haven’t even given each other a side-eyed look, despite playing so many hotly contested games in the regular season and postseason.</p><p>Where’s the fun in that?</p><p>“It’s interesting that there can be both intensity, but not like it turns into other stuff too much,” Cubs infielder Nico Hoerner told the Sun-Times. “Both teams play the game pretty hard, but I don’t feel like either team is dirty.”</p><p>The Cubs are going to finish second to the Brewers in the National League Central for the fourth consecutive year and the third straight under manager Craig Counsell, whom they poached from the Brewers to beat them. Doesn’t that irritate anyone in the Cubs’ clubhouse?</p><p>“I know a lot of the guys on that team,” Cubs shortstop Dansby Swanson told us. “It’s hard to have animosity toward good people.”</p><p>Maybe that’s why. There’s no one on either team who gets under the skin of the other team.</p><p>“There hasn’t been a moment of pettiness or bad blood,” Hoerner said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/OyuoZW2pS6w?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="Coaches get into a fight near third base"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>There could have been Monday. Cubs superstar Pete Crow-Armstrong led off the game with a bouncer to first baseman Andrew Vaughn, who bobbled the ball, stepped on the bag and got bowled over by Crow-Armstrong, who had nowhere to go.</p><p>But instead of igniting an all-out melee, Crow-Armstrong tried to soften Vaughn’s fall, put his arm around him and made sure he was OK.</p><p>What are these, the Friendship Games?</p><p>“There was no extra shove or anything like that,” Cubs pitcher Colin Rea, who has been on both sides of the rivalry — or whatever this is — told us. “It was an accident. If that was 20 years ago, he would have tried to take him out. But it’s just not the way the game is played right now.”</p><p>“Vaughn’s a great dude,” Swanson said. “I signed a bat for something he’s doing at his house.”</p><p>Maybe it stems from the managers, who have a decadeslong relationship. Brewers manager Pat Murphy was Cubs manager Craig Counsell’s coach at Notre Dame. When Counsell managed the Brewers, Murphy was his bench coach — for all nine seasons.</p><p>“They have a long history with each other. They have a good relationship,” Rea said. “Yeah, I think it could stem from that. If they didn’t get along, maybe that would trickle down to the players.”</p><p>Like it did for the Bears and Packers under former coaches Mike Ditka and Forrest Gregg, respectively, in the 1980s. Their relationship — or whatever it was — more closely resembled Bevington-Garner, without the fisticuffs. Though they did get into a shouting match — during a preseason game.</p><p>This is all to say that, while the Cubs and Brewers compete to the hilt against each other, they don’t dislike each other. At all.</p><p>Pity.</p><p>“There’s definitely competitiveness, talk amongst the team as far as how badly we want to win,” Rea said. “Being around that side, all those guys are great guys, and I see the same thing in this clubhouse. We have two very similar teams, so it’s hard to dislike guys on that team.”</p><p>“It’s not like animosity towards them as much as it is a great challenge for us to rise to the occasion,” Swanson said.<br></p>
entries.author: Jeff Agrest

entries.title: Sean Burke shelled as White Sox need quick answers for their flagging starting rotation
entries.summary: <p>Beginning with 7⅓ innings of one-run ball on June 18, Sean Burke put together a seven-outing run of a 1.42 ERA over 50⅔ innings, establishing the right-hander as the stabilizing force in a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> starting rotation that sorely needed one.</p><p>On Tuesday night, with the Sox guarding a slim lead in the AL Central, the first seven Pirates hitters Burke faced all reached base. The first five balls put in play off the 26-year-old all sizzled off the bat at 99.5 mph or harder, and the score was lopsided before the clock hit 7 p.m.</p><p>After issuing eight walks in his outing before last, which he called “the worst athletic performance of my life,” Burke yielded a career-high seven runs on eight hits in a career-low 1⅓ innings against the Pirates, departing after walking the bases loaded in the second to a mix of jeers and supportive applause befitting a breakout star whose brilliance has helped make White Sox games in September relevant, and whose suddenly erratic performance made it distressing.</p><p>Despite the carnage, Burke’s 3.58 ERA and 156 innings both still pace the Sox rotation. That’s in spite of him not recording a quality start in his last five outings, though <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/01/white-sox-prospect-tanner-mcdougal-looking-to-show-improved-mechanics-after-rocky-debut-colson-montgomery-davis-martin-will-venable" target="_blank" ><u>his 5⅔ scoreless innings in Houston last week</u></a> came as close as possible.</p><p>But that reflects the shaky state of a White Sox rotation already at the bottom of the league in total innings. Davis Martin made a strong return from the injured list last week, but Anthony Kay has failed to complete five innings in his last three outings, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/03/white-sox-keeping-luis-castillo-in-rotation-and-munetaka-murakami-high-in-batting-order-amid-struggles-will-venable-astros-road-trip-zach-bove-al-central-division-playoffs" target="_blank" ><u>Luis Castillo has a 7.25 ERA since being acquired last month</u></a>, and manager Will Venable used a bullpen game to seize a rubber match victory from the Twins on Sunday.</p><p>With the way Sox starters are stumbling near the season’s finish line, Venable could go that route again soon.</p><p>“That's a good indication of what it could look like,” said Venable, who indicated his pitcher usage might have the all-hands-on-deck flavor of a playoff series down the stretch. “We've got some pretty special arms [in the bullpen] that can obviously get swing and miss, get some outs. But they can do it over multiple innings."</p><p>Burke has rejected the notion that fatigue is a factor in his recent mechanical inconsistency, even with his prior professional career-high in innings in the rearview mirror. Sox pitching coaches indicated that Burke’s emergence this year has been helped by dropping his arm slot, reducing the frequency with which his breaking balls pop up out of his hand on release and reveal themselves to opposing hitters.</p><p>To even further simplify the cue to something that lines up with his best command, Burke informs that when his shoulders remain level with each other throughout his delivery, his pitches are more consistent. When it’s awry, as it has been recently, he can spiral.</p><p>“Getting a little bit out of slot, I have a bad habit when you can’t command the ball well, of <i>trying</i> to get the ball there,” Burke told the Sun-Times last week. “That just makes it worse, because you’re diving your body forward and your arm can be later again.”</p><p>Last week in Houston, Burke made the correction quickly enough to salvage a great outing. On Tuesday, things spiraled for Burke too quickly for any mid-game adjustment, and far too swiftly for a Sox offense that didn’t manage a baserunner off Pirates starter Bubba Chandler until the fifth inning.</p><p>With the Cleveland Guardians on their heels, the Sox need to restore a better version of Burke over the season’s final 2½ weeks, as he’s spent most of 2026 looking like the closest thing they have to a rotation anchor.</p><p>“There's this extra gear that he's shown flashes of,” said pitching coach Zach Bove. “He can do that at a high level for many more years to come.”</p>

entries.title: Former White Sox' first-round pick Jacob Gonzalez returns to Rate Field after being traded in July
entries.summary: <p>Infielder <b>Jacob Gonzalez</b> was a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox" >White Sox</a> first-round pick in 2023 and leading the minors in homers when he was called up earlier this year, but still suspected he could be the odd man out.</p><p>“I was always nervous,” Gonzalez told the Sun-Times on Tuesday, before his first game at Rate Field since being traded to the Pirates in July. “What’s going to happen when [<b>Munetaka Murakami</b>] comes back?”</p><p>A drastically reworked swing under hitting director <b>Ryan Fuller</b>’s tutelage, a blistering .317/.419/.668 start in Triple-A, and Murakami’s Grade 2 hamstring strain, all worked to grant the 24-year-old Gonzalez a 30-game run with the White Sox. He was no Murakami, posting a .683 OPS while manning first base in his stead, but showed mettle in batting 8-for-18 (.444) with runners in scoring position; including a June 27 walk-off single against the Royals.</p><p>Still, the writing was on the wall when Murakami returned. Gonzalez was optioned to Charlotte as the corresponding move, and when he was pulled two innings into his first game back in the minors, he didn’t think it was for a return trip to Chicago.</p><p>“I didn't get told until the game ended what happened, so I was just sitting in the clubhouse waiting,” Gonzalez said. “I had enough time to figure out I was probably traded, but just sitting around and not knowing anything, that was the craziest part.”</p><p>Rather than infield depth, the Sox felt Gonzalez’s 2026 turnaround from looking like a failed prospect was best used to acquire more draft capital. They traded Gonzalez and lefty <b>Brandon Eisert</b> to Pittsburgh for relief prospect <b>Jaden Woods</b> and the 34th overall pick, which they used on Nazareth Academy shortstop <b>Landon Thome</b>.</p><p>Acquired to give the Pirates a shortstop while <b>Konnor Griffin</b> was out with an injury, Gonzalez hasn’t yet inspired regret. Entering Tuesday, Gonzalez has a .595 OPS with Pittsburgh, and is bouncing around the infield now that Griffin has returned. Gonzalez still stays in touch with his old teammates, and is even planning a December trip to Japan with <b>Sam Antonacci, Rikuu Nishida</b> and others, but betrayed no big emotions about returning to where it started.</p><p>“Feels like a normal road trip for me, but it’ll be fun to play against some of my friends,” said Gonzalez, who appreciates looking over his shoulder less at his new place. “It’s probably been better for me to come up here and struggle a bit, because that means I got to figure some new things out.”</p><h3><b>Brazoban at the ready</b></h3><p>Acquired at last month’s trade deadline to boost the bullpen, right-hander <b>Huascar Brazoban</b> is back in Chicago after two scoreless appearances in his Triple-A rehab assignment for a left lat strain. But the White Sox aren’t rushing him back into action.</p><p>“He's on the taxi squad right now,” said manager <b>Will Venable</b> “In case there's a need over the next couple of days, he'll be close by.”</p><p>Brazoban had yielded runs in five of his last six appearances prior to his injury.</p><h3><b>Dash in playoffs, sans Wolkow</b></h3><p>The Winston-Salem Dash, the Sox’ High-A affiliate, began a best-of-three series against Bowling Green in the South Atlantic League playoffs. They’re playing without 20-year-old Downers Grove-native <b>George Wolkow</b>, who posted a 22-homer, 100-RBI season, after he suffered a hairline fracture of his left big toe on a slide.</p>

entries.title: Ranking the 10 best senior basketball players in Illinois
entries.summary: <p>The prospect rankings in the Class of 2027 in Illinois are unlike any other year in state history.</p><p>Simply put, the college commitments and recruiting lists for players ranked in the top 10 in Illinois aren’t anywhere near the level we’ve ever seen. Just one example: It’s the Ivy League and mid-major conferences — not the Big Ten — battling for the state’s top talent.</p><p>But there will always be an asterisk attached to this class.</p><p>Keep in mind, there are five nationally ranked players who will all be headed to high-major programs who began their high school basketball careers in Illinois.</p><p>The names are familiar, including Davion Thompson (Bolingbrook), who actually has reclassified and is a freshman at Arkansas, Devin Cleveland (Kenwood), Jaxson Davis (Warren), Howard Williams (Young) and Illinois commit Quinton Kitt (East Peoria). They all left for prep schools.</p><p>As a result, here are the top 10 prospects as they begin their senior year.</p><h3>1. Ed Stasys, Benet</h3><p>Stasys has earned his unexpected rise to the top spot. After an impressive spring and summer full of production, the ultra-competitive 6-8 big man is set to show he’s more than just an elite defensive player and rebounder with toughness.</p><h3>2. Mason Martin, Neuqua Valley</h3><p>The best shooter in the class boasts size at 6-4 and a quick release to go with his unlimited range. Adding strength and evolving his game will come in time for the Illinois commit.</p><h3>3. J’dyn Lloyd, Belleville West</h3><h3></h3><p>A physically imposing player with athletic gifts, the 6-5 Lloyd certainly looks the part. But an improved jumper and consistency elevated his stock. He’s committed to Missouri State.</p><h3>4. Alex Sirbu, Buffalo Grove</h3><h3></h3><p>From the time this class entered high school, there might not be a more improved player than the 6-9 Sirbu. An elite rebounder with size and strength, Sirbu is headed to Columbia in the Ivy League over other mid-major opportunities.</p><h3>5. Jamier Montgomery, Crane</h3><h3></h3><p>What a spectacular few weeks the smooth combo scoring guard put together in June and July. He grabbed a lot of worthy attention and was an instant mid-major target, ultimately committing to Kent State.</p><h3>6. Hayden Schroeder, Wheaton Academy</h3><h3></h3><p>All the 6-7 Schroeder has done throughout his career is produce. And he does his offensive damage with his back to the basket and with an improving face-up jumper.</p><h3>7. Mikey Woods, Perspectives-Leadership</h3><p>He’s new to the city and to the rankings, returning to Chicago after playing his freshman year at St. Francis de Sales. But he’s a high-motor, aggressive and talented guard with Division I ability.</p><h3>8. Markese Peoples, St. Laurence</h3><h3></h3><p>A breakout junior year was followed by an impressive spring that warranted more attention. It’s so difficult to divert the physical, big-bodied guard from the basket. Headed to Central Michigan.</p><h3>9. Kendall Meyers, Marist</h3><h3></h3><p>A seasoned player who helped the RedHawks to a state title last season, look for the 6-5 jack-of-all-trades Meyers to blossom as a senior as his role and opportunity expands.</p><h3>10. Ryan Howard, Alton</h3><h3></h3><p>A versatile and underrated player in the southern part of the state who impacts the game in a variety of ways and affects winning. Howard is staying close to home and headed to SIUE.</p>

entries.title: Jacob Webb blows another save before Brewers walk-off Cubs in 10 innings
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE — No one is walking through the Cubs’ clubhouse door to save their bullpen. Not Randy Myers, Rod Beck, Carlos Marmol or Lee Smith. Certainly not anyone from Triple-A Iowa, according to manager Craig Counsell.</p><p>“The answers are not there,” he said. “These are our guys. They’re the guys we’re going to rely on. We’ve got to figure it out.”</p><p>That has been easier said than done this series against the Brewers. After Carson Kelly hit a go-ahead two-run double in the ninth inning Tuesday night at American Family Field, closer Jacob Webb gave it back in the bottom half of the inning, allowing a two-out, two-run homer to the Brewers’ Jackson Chourio. Caleb Thielbar lost it in the 10th on Luis Lara’s bases-loaded single, and the Cubs lost 4-3 to fall nine games back of the Brewers.</p><p>The bigger issue is in the National League wild-card race, where the Cubs (81-56) now trail the Phillies by a half-game for the top spot and lead the surging Diamondbacks by only three games.</p><p>Since going 24 outings without allowing a run, Webb has allowed nine runs in his last six. He has blown three saves in that span, the first two on two-out, walk-off homers. At least here, only one runner was on base.</p><p>“I’m tired of letting the team down, to be completely honest,” Webb said. “It’s pretty tough to watch every time I give up a homer.”</p><p>Said Counsell: “It’s the one thing that can’t happen there. Unfortunately, it happened.”</p><p>Webb began the ninth by fanning Joey Ortiz. Garrett Mitchell then lined out to center field. But Webb allowed a line-drive single by pinch hitter Christian Yelich before Chourio smashed an 0-1 changeup into the left-field seats.</p><p>“It comes down to location, execution,” Webb said. “I’m not doing that currently.”</p><p>Counsell noted: “He’s made some bad pitches with his off-speed. It’s been the off-speed to right-handed hitters.”</p><p>Thielbar, who has struggled for much of the season, began the 10th by striking out Jake Bauers. After intentionally walking Willson Contreras, he allowed a single that fell between left fielder Matt Shaw and shortstop Nico Hoerner and another to Lara.</p><p>Perhaps Ian Happ would have gotten to that ball if he were still in the game. He fouled a pitch off his foot and had to leave, prompting Counsell to move Shaw from second to left, where he had played only twice this season.</p><p>The Cubs’ bullpen had done the job until the ninth. Trent Thornton, Aaron Civale and Ryan Rolison combined for 3⅔ scoreless innings after David Peterson allowed one run in 4⅓. Brewers phenom Jacob Misiorowski allowed one run in 6 ⅓ innings, and the game stayed 1-1 until Kelly’s hit against closer Trevor Megill.</p><p>“Carson had an incredible at-bat to give us the lead,” Counsell said. “And then we made a bad pitch with a man on base.”</p><p>By the sound of it, Webb will have a chance to redeem himself — again.</p><p>“I think we’re going to get back on track,” he said. “I have confidence in myself.”</p><p></p><p><b>NOTES: </b>Cubs star <b>Pete Crow-Armstrong</b> snapped his hitless streak against <b>Jacob Misiorowski</b>. With only two walks in his first 17 career plate appearances against “The Miz,” he singled in No. 18. He has struck out against Misiorowski nine times.</p><p>• <b>Craig Counsell</b> said shortstop <b>Dansby Swanson</b> (oblique) will have “some kind of game action, we think, during the Atlanta series” next week. That means Swanson could have a rehab assignment at Iowa or play in a simulated game. He could return during the series in Cincinnati that follows.</p><p>• Right-hander <b>Shelby Miller</b> (elbow) and left-hander <b>Justin Steele</b> (elbow) were scheduled to pitch Wednesday and Thursday, respectively, at Triple-A Iowa. Righties <b>Gavin Hollowell </b>(shoulder) and <b>Edward Cabrera </b>(finger blister) saw their outings Tuesday at Iowa rained out.</p>

entries.title: Girl, 6, dies after struck by school bus in Frankfort
entries.summary: <p>A 6-year-old girl died Tuesday after she was struck by a school bus in suburban Frankfort, police said. </p><p>Officers at about 3:24 p.m. responded to the 500 block of Aberdeen Road and found the child unresponsive at the location after being hit by the bus, police said in a news release. </p><p>Witnesses and first responders at the scene attempted to revive the girl before she was transported by ambulance to a local hospital, where she later died, police said. </p><p>Investigators indicated that the bus contained several passengers at the time of the collision, but no other injuries were reported. </p><p>"This tragic incident has had a profound impact on those involved, their families, and our community. We extend our deepest sympathies to everyone affected by this heartbreaking event," Frankfort police said in a statement. "Our thoughts and prayers are with the victim, their family, loved ones, and all those impacted as they navigate this difficult time."</p><p>This investigation remains ongoing, police said. </p>

entries.title: Ultimate Bears QB1? Former quarterbacks discuss who was the best
entries.summary: <p>From 1990 to 1993, Bears fans knew Jim Harbaugh was their starting quarterback. There was even greater certainty from 2009 to 2016, the Jay Cutler years. For 15 seasons in between, though, the Bears’ quarterback picture changed so often it was like staring into a carnival house of mirrors.</p><p>Over that decade and a half, the Bears had, if you can believe it, 11 different players lead them in passing yards for a season. Erik Kramer did it three times (1995, ’97, ’98); Jim Miller (2001, ’02) and Kyle Orton (2005, ’08) twice each. Also mixed in were Steve Walsh, Dave Krieg, Shane Matthews, Cade McNown, Kordell Stewart, Chad Hutchinson, Rex Grossman and Brian Griese.</p><p>As this year’s Bears — led by one of the most promising QBs in the NFL, Caleb Williams — were hard at it in training camp, five of Williams’ predecessors talked with the Sun-Times about the team’s history at the position. Kramer, 61, was in Southern California getting his latest round of youth football camps off the ground. Miller, 55, was sorting out what comes next in his broadcasting career. Orton, 43, was in the insurance business in his native Iowa. Walsh, 59, was fundraising for his high school in Minnesota, where he recently hung up the coaching whistle. And Matthews, 56, was podcasting and prepping for another season as a radio color analyst at his alma mater, Florida. Their words have been lightly edited to include key facts such as years, opponents, etc.</p><h3><b>Who’s the best Bears QB of them all?</b></h3><p><b>Miller:</b> You’re always going to say Jim McMahon because he got a championship, right? Whether or not it was because of the defense and the running game, he was obviously a good leader and the team followed him. Probably the most talented was Jay Cutler, but he just didn’t get it done. I probably would put Caleb at three.</p><p><b>Orton:</b> I guess I would preface it by saying I’m not, like, a football historian and might miss one of the really early guys, but Jim McMahon in my mind would be the best of all. The Super Bowl. I don’t know him, but he seems like he brought great leadership and a persona to the offense. He had a different kind of energy.</p><p><b>Walsh:</b> You can’t argue with a ring and a championship, and that points to Jimmy Mac. Even though he was injured a lot because of the way he played, rings are hard to dispute.</p><p><b>Matthews:</b> You’ve obviously got to put McMahon first. He won the Super Bowl. Rex got the Bears there as well, and Erik Kramer put up huge numbers, so you have to mention them. But probably the most talented one of all of them is Caleb Williams. He is a great thrower of the football and has great mobility.</p><h3><b>Where will Williams end up in the pecking order?</b></h3><p><b>Kramer:</b> He’s probably the most physically talented quarterback the Bears have ever had, so he’s got that going for him. He probably has the best offensive-minded coach we’ve seen in a long time, too; I think Ben Johnson is right up there with Sean McVay for sure. There won’t even be a close second to Caleb when it’s all said and done. I think last year will be the worst year he’s had for at least the next seven or eight years.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure on Monday, Sept. 8, 2025.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Ashlee Rezin/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p><b>Matthews:</b> If he stays healthy — and with Ben Johnson calling the plays — he’s got a chance to be No. 1 on the list. Ben is one of the best schemers and play-callers in the league. If Caleb is healthy and stays a Bear for a long time, he could be that franchise quarterback they’ve been looking for for a long time.</p><p>But whoever the trigger man is needs good players around him, a good football team. Different franchises have had Hall of Famers, great QBs — just look at the Packers — but I think the Bears have had a lot of QBs who weren’t stars. I was an undrafted free agent. Great quarterbacks don’t just fall off trees.</p><p><b>Walsh:</b> This is a pivotal season for a lot of these young quarterbacks, not just Caleb but Jayden Daniels, C.J. Stroud, a lot of guys. They’ve all had good moments and they’re talented, athletic, but the key to long-term elite quarterback play is going to be consistency.</p><p>Can Caleb go out this year with maybe even more on his shoulders — because he’s proven he can handle it at times — and make the right decisions, make the critical play, stay healthy, handle all that? You can’t just say, ‘Oh, he’s going to be the best.’ He’s got to prove it on the field. That’s not done in one year. He had an average rookie year and spectacular comebacks in his second year. Can he back it up in his third year?</p><p><b>Orton:</b> He’s got a super-high ceiling. I’d say for early on he has everything he needs — playmakers, talent, great coach, great system — to be a special player. With good things around him, who knows how good he could be?</p><p><b>Miller:</b> I think he’ll be the Bears’ all-time leader in passing, I really do. He’s got a ton of skills and the ability to improvise, and he’s with a good play-caller. I think Caleb is smart enough to understand that Ben Johnson is good for him. If he pays attention, he probably will emerge as the Bears’ best QB of all time.</p><h3><b>Why haven’t the Bears had better play and more long-term success at the position?</b></h3><p><b>Orton:</b> I’m no front-office expert, but certainly in the time I was associated there — and for a long time before and after — I would say a majority of the salary cap was used on the defensive side of the ball. If you’re not going to go get a $150 million QB, then you probably won’t have a wide receiver and a left tackle to go with it. In the NFL, kind of just follow the money.</p><p><b>Miller:</b> When you go back and look at the quarterbacks drafted in the first round — McNown (1999), Grossman (2003), whoever — you’ve got to surround young QBs with weapons. You can’t expect them to just take over the team. The Bears have always been defense, the “Monsters.” Now, Caleb has kind of flipped the script. Colston Loveland, Luther Burden, Rome Odunze, Joe Thuney — these are not your grandfather’s Chicago Bears. This is an offensive team now. This is an offensive league now.</p><p><b>Walsh:</b> With the Bears, it’s going back to how George Halas established the identity of the franchise. Gritty, tough defense led the way for a long time. There just was a style of play that permeated throughout the franchise that doesn’t lead to big stats from the quarterback position.</p><p>You were Bears teammates with a lot of pretty good QBs — fairly notable names — but none of them became stars or locked down the job. What was that like?</p><p><b>Orton:</b> Man, very choppy. Coming out my rookie year, I started (15 games in 2005). Then, I think, the next season I was back to No. 3 on the depth chart. It was so hard to establish leadership, hard to establish consistency within that job. You never felt like you could get comfortable, for sure.</p><p><b>Matthews:</b> All those guys, none of them were the superstar-type QBs you have to have at any level to win big, right? People talk about the NFL Draft, but the majority are going to be busts because they don’t turn into that superstar QB everybody’s striving to find. It was just one guy after another. It wasn’t great.</p><h3><b>What was your best game, moment or memory as a Bear?</b></h3><p><b>Walsh:</b> The playoff game in Minnesota to beat the Vikings (35-18 on Jan. 1, 1995) after they had beaten us twice during the season — obviously a lot of things went well that day, and I played well — is high in my register of memories.</p><p>But another game earlier that year, playing Detroit in Soldier Field, our whole game plan was to keep the ball away from [Lions running back] Barry Sanders. I remember going on monster drives in that game. (The Bears had three scoring drives of at least 15 plays and possessed the ball for 44:12 in a 20-10 win.) We controlled the clock and just kept them off the field. We set out with a plan and executed it perfectly. I didn’t throw for a lot of yards, but I completed a high amount of my passes and everything just felt right. That was a good day.</p><p><b>Matthews:</b> It had to be the miraculous <a class="Link" href="https://youtu.be/suNImV3suqE?si=MiUrhv6R7_o-Lbo2" target="_blank" >comeback against the Browns in 2001, </a>with the Hail Mary and winning the game in OT (27-21, after Matthews threw two touchdown passes — with an onside kick recovery sandwiched between them — in the final half-minute of regulation). And the week before that, we had the comeback against the 49ers. (Matthews came off the bench to lead the Bears from a 28-9 deficit to a 37-31 overtime win. Incredibly, safety Mike Brown ended both games with interception returns for touchdowns.)</p><p>I had my moments, but I wasn’t the prototypical QB. I was 6-3, 190, didn’t have a strong arm. I probably should have been a coach and not a player.</p><p><b>Orton:</b> I played a pretty long time (10 years, with five teams), but my best memories of my career are with the Bears. I never wanted to leave that place. I loved my teammates, loved the fans, some of our comeback wins, improbable stuff because of our special teams and defense. It was the greatest locker-room environment I’ve ever been a part of, with the greatest superstar leader I’ve even been around in (Hall of Fame linebacker) Brian Urlacher.</p><p><b>Miller:</b> When Tampa had their great defenses, we beat them twice in one year (27-24 and 27-3 in 2001, with Miller starting both games). For me, it was just about managing the game, managing the clock. Winning a tight affair is a big challenge because you cannot have the costly mistake that costs your team the game.</p><p>We were a good team that year, 13-3 and won the division. entries.title: For the first time in CB Jaylon Johnson's Bears career, he believes the Super Bowl is a 'tangible' goal
entries.summary: <p>A book about cornerback Jaylon Johnson’s time with <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >the Bears</a> would have every possible kind of drama. Things can get pretty wild at Halas Hall sometimes, but his tenure has truly been unique.</p><p>Since being drafted at age 21, he has played for three head coaches and five defensive coordinators. He was on one of their worst teams ever in 2022 and the one last season that won a playoff game for the first time in 15 years.</p><p>He requested a trade, then walked it back and signed a contract extension — revealing his innermost personal struggles at the news conference to announce it. He also <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2024/12/02/bears-cb-jaylon-johnson-says-of-post-game-confrontation-with-matt-eberflus-enough-is-enough" >led a locker-room revolt against former coach Matt Eberflus</a> that helped the Bears realize it was time to fire him.</p><p>And, going into Year 7, this story is “still being written,” Johnson pointed out.</p><p>“I don’t even think about how crazy it is,” he told the Sun-Times. “You just took me down memory lane, but I’m just where my feet are.</p><p>“And right now, this is the most confident, talented team we’ve had since I’ve been here and we have an opportunity to do something special. Bluntly speaking, we’ve never had the Super Bowl just being talked about as a tangible item for us here.”</p><p>Bears coach <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/09/01/the-bears-and-their-fans-needed-a-truth-teller-they-got-one-in-new-coach-ben-johnson" >Ben Johnson</a> has kept that ambition central as his team approaches its season opener Sunday at the Panthers. The Bears won the division last season and reached the second round of the playoffs, so the natural next step would be title contention.</p><p>While belief abounds in the offense, however, the Bears’ defense causes pause. It was unreliable last season, albeit with Jaylon Johnson sidelined by a core-muscle injury for most of it, and there are just as many questions going into this season.</p><p>Jaylon Johnson could answer some of those if he returns to the lockdown corner he was when he made the Pro Bowl in 2023 and ’24 and gave the Bears a solution to any opponent’s star wide receiver.</p><p>They arguably need him now more than ever. Fellow outside cornerback Tyrique Stevenson could go either way. Nickel corner Kyler Gordon isn’t around. On the back end, the Bears are trusting journeyman Xavier Woods and rookie Dillon Thieneman at safety.</p><p>It starts with being right physically, and Johnson was far from it when he returned from surgery late last season. He gave what he could, but he wasn’t his usual self.</p><p>Then he clocked 21 miles per hour on a sprint at the beginning of training camp, a good sign. He has continued to improve, but has never quite considered himself all the way back.</p><p>“I’m getting there, getting to where I’m comfortable,” he said. “But I still feel myself getting stronger, getting better, and I’m always going to leave some room for improvement.”</p><p>He’ll get a decent test against Panthers wide receiver Tetairoa McMillan, who was the offensive rookie of the year last season. He hasn’t earned the glowing reviews Johnson has given to superstars, but he credited McMillan as “somebody you’ve got to respect.”</p><p>He mentions respect often. He gives so much weight to concept of earning it and using it well. It took time even for Ben Johnson to earn his respect, because Jaylon Johnson had heard it all before from new coaches, but he has it now in part because their goals are aligned.</p><p>He listened intently when Ben Johnson pulled him aside in training camp and said he needed more from him, both at cornerback and as an essential voice within the team.</p><p>Ben Johnson said Tuesday he “could feel a fire lit under” Jaylon Johnson the last few weeks, and Jaylon hinted that their conversation coincided with that spark. Late in camp, Jaylon interrupted a practice, called the players together and challenged their effort. The energy surged. He’s an elite cornerback, sure, but he can bring a lot more to the Bears this season.</p>

entries.title: Curbing pay-to-play in Chicago politics
entries.summary: <p>Three years ago, the Chicago Board of Ethics introduced a set of reforms that would strengthen the city's ethics rules. Nearly three years later, 47th Ward Ald. Matt Martin's ordinance incorporating those reforms is still waiting for a vote, as city leadership dragged its feet instead of advancing common-sense corruption-fighting measures.</p><p>That may finally change Wednesday, when Martin's legislation is expected to come before the City Council's <a class="Link" href="https://occprodstoragev1.blob.core.usgovcloudapi.net/meetingattachmentspublic/bc265d9a-3c6f-4fea-956c-04341b01f1bd.pdf" target="_blank" >Ethics and Government Oversight Committee.</a></p><p>One key provision, however, has been pulled from the ordinance in an effort to improve its chances of passage: closing a major loophole in limits on political donations to candidates from city contractors.</p><p>Currently, companies doing business with the city are limited to $1,500 in donations to city candidates. But the owners, partners, directors and officers of those companies face no such limit — meaning the same interests the law is meant to restrain can simply route their money through individuals instead.</p><p>This isn't just a theoretical problem. A Better Government Association <a class="Link" href="https://www.bettergov.org/2024/02/15/campaign-cash-from-city-contractors-target-of-new-ethics-ordinance/" target="_blank" >analysis</a> of political spending in Chicago found hundreds of thousands of dollars in donations that would have been illegal under the stricter limits other major cities already enforce.</p><p>The loophole makes a mockery of a critical safeguard against the pay-to-play politics that have plagued Chicago for decades, including the <a class="Link" href="https://projects.suntimes.com/uncategorized/from-hired-trucks-to-homicide-much-that-daley-faced-in-2004-took-years-to-surface/index.html" target="_blank" >Hired Truck scanda</a>l, when big donors to Mayor Richard M. Daley received millions of dollars in city contracts and did little or no work, with some even stealing asphalt paid for by taxpayers to use on private jobs.</p><p>Major cities including New York and Los Angeles have already closed this loophole. Chicago should, too.</p><p>The City Council should advance Martin's ordinance and finally put these long-awaited ethics reforms into law. But the contractor contribution provision remains an important piece of unfinished business. We hope Council members will revisit it soon and close a loophole that leaves Chicago's safeguards against pay-to-play politics weaker than they should be.</p><p><i>Alisa Kaplan</i><b><i>, </i></b><i>executive director, Reform for Illinois</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-fe0000" name="module-fe0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3><b>Data center moratorium could cost Chicago </b></h3><p>Mayor Brandon Johnson’s push for a <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/11/mayor-brandon-johnson-chicago-moratorium-data-centers-new-regulations" >temporary moratorium</a> on new data centers risks becoming another example of Chicago officials making today’s politics tomorrow’s problem.</p><p>Johnson signed an executive order calling for new regulations within 90 days and urged the City Council to halt new projects while those rules are developed.</p><p>Any pause must remain temporary. Chicago has seen the long-term cost of moratoriums. A ban on school closures left Chicago Public Schools with fewer options as enrollment fell and deficits returned. Illinois also <a class="Link" href="https://www.illinoispolicy.org/nuclear-energy-gives-illinois-economic-power-if-it-will-allow-new-plants/" target="_blank" >prohibited new large-scale nuclear plants</a> for four decades as electricity demand grew.</p><p>Imagine how much better-positioned Illinois would have been to meet rising electricity demand had previous lawmakers allowed expansion of the state’s nuclear advantage instead of passing a moratorium.</p><p>Chicago should now apply that lesson to data centers by addressing concerns without cutting off future development. A City Council working group has released <a class="Link" href="https://blockclubchicago.org/2026/08/06/data-centers-should-be-required-to-disclose-water-and-energy-use-city-panel-recommends/" target="_blank" >recommendations that can be adopted</a> with necessary environmental and community safeguards.</p><p>Chicago’s climate, underused properties and abundant nuclear power make it well suited for tech developments. Existing data centers<a class="Link" href="https://www.protectingtaxpayers.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/Illinois.pdf" target="_blank" ><u> </u>account</a> for less than 0.5% of the state’s water use, while<a class="Link" href="https://www.theatlantic.com/technology/2026/07/how-much-water-data-centers-use/687934/" target="_blank" > newer designs</a> can reduce that footprint further. A moratorium would not eliminate demand. It would send investment elsewhere despite Chicago’s natural advantages.</p><p>Data centers <a class="Link" href="https://www.gatech.edu/news/2026/07/09/data-centers-are-booming-who-benefits" target="_blank" >increase</a> employment, wages and business formation in urban areas. An investor wants to convert part of <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/13/loop-data-center-gabal-landmarked-office-building" target="_blank" >300 W. Adams St.</a> in the Loop, which was almost 60% vacant in 2023, into a data center. The project has received preliminary landmarks approval and would bring its own electrical infrastructure and investment to the aging property.</p><p>Policymakers should keep the city competitive for similar investments without providing <a class="Link" href="https://www.chicagotribune.com/2026/08/23/special-report-data-centers-taxes/" target="_blank" >property tax breaks</a> that shift the burden onto homeowners.</p><p>Moratoriums delay difficult questions. Good policy resolves them.</p><p><i>Micky Horstman, communications manager, Illinois Policy Institute, and social mobility fellow, Young Voices </i></p><h3>Breaking the ICE </h3><p>Dear ICE:<br>a pestilence we did not request<br>pollution to our lungs<br>a vermin we cannot expel</p><p>to the refugee<br>you are the war criminal<br>to the asylum seeker<br>you are a terror<br>to the immigrant<br>you are the shameless thief</p><p>you are not welcome here<br>in Albany Park<br>in Chicago<br>on our streets<br>In our neighborhoods</p><p>we shall not rest until you are disarmed<br>may our chanting ring in your ears:<br>HANDS OFF<br>¡FUERA ICE!</p><p><i>Christine Anderson, Jefferson Park</i></p><h3>Don’t impose church’s views </h3><p>The Catholic Church has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2026/09/03/cardinal-blase-cupich-chicago-archdiocese-nuns-challenge-right-to-die-law-assisted-suicide" >challenged</a> Illinois' so-called <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2025/11/03/illinois-right-to-die-bill-pritzker" target="_blank" >“right-to-die” legislation<u>,</u></a> arguing in part that the law violates First Amendment's religious freedom and free speech rights</p><p>The Catholic Church has the right to practice religion as it wishes and to require that followers adhere to the practices required by the church. The Catholic Church has every right to decide that Catholics cannot avail themselves of the law and be considered a practicing Catholic. The church can state that availing oneself of the law is a sin against God. I have no problem with the church saying and doing this.</p><p>I do have a problem with the Catholic Church arguing that it has the right to impose its beliefs on me — a person who is not Catholic and not a member of its church. Under the First Amendment, the church has no right to impose its religious views on me. The decision, if it ever comes, for me to decide to seek physician-assisted suicide is between my family and me. </p><p>I don’t want or need the church to impose its view on me. The Catholic Church needs to concern itself with its followers and stop trying to impose its views on nonpractitioners.</p><p><i>Peter Felitti. Lincoln Square</i> </p>

entries.title: Sept. 11-spawned surveillance is ravaging the country
entries.summary: <p>Twenty-five years ago, my family prepared to move out of the West Ridge home where I had grown up. We hadn’t yet closed on our new house, so we had plans to stay put and rent our old place for six months from the new owners.</p><p>But after Sept. 11, 2001, the buyers informed my Pakistani American Muslim family that we needed to vacate the home by the end of the month. With my brother and me out of town for college, my parents were forced to pack up our lives by themselves and move into my uncle’s basement.</p><p>In the mad rush to empty the house, my parents started throwing out personal belongings they couldn't take. Some suspicious neighbors scrutinized their activities and started digging through our trash.</p><p>After stumbling upon the flight logs from dad's flying lessons from the mid-1970s, a neighbor called the FBI. On the day my parents handed the keys to the new homeowners, my dad was forced to make a trip Downtown to the Rock ‘n’ Roll McDonald’s where he explained to FBI agents that flying was a hobby he took up during his early years in Chicago. </p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-750000" name="module-750000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Commentary bug</div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Commentary</h2></div> </div><p>My mom, on her way to my uncle's, was terrified that my dad would be disappeared, like so many other Muslim men in the aftermath of 9/11.</p><p>My dad, who had previously worked as an engineer for Pakistan International Airlines, was free to go once the FBI agents realized he wasn't a threat. The nosy neighbors never apologized. Neither did the FBI.</p><p>That was my family’s first taste of the emerging surveillance state, which enveloped our country after 9/11 and has been normalized ever since. As the so-called global war on terrorism expanded, surveillance became more sophisticated. Busybody neighbors have been replaced by Big Tech conglomerates digging through our online data instead.</p><p>And yet, very few bat an eye. </p><p>From the USA Patriot Act to the National Security Agency’s illegal wiretapping of activists, most Americans have grown accustomed to our government spying on them.</p><p>While the initial focus was on Muslims and Arabs, the surveillance regime has also targeted the <a class="Link" href="https://theintercept.com/2015/07/24/documents-show-department-homeland-security-monitoring-black-lives-matter-since-ferguson/" target="_blank" >Movement for Black Lives</a>, water protectors at the <a class="Link" href="https://theintercept.com/2017/05/27/leaked-documents-reveal-security-firms-counterterrorism-tactics-at-standing-rock-to-defeat-pipeline-insurgencies/" target="_blank" >Standing Rock</a> reservation fighting to stop the Dakota Access Pipeline and <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2012/12/25/nyregion/occupy-movement-was-investigated-by-fbi-counterterrorism-agents-records-show.html" target="_blank" >Occupy Wall Street</a> activists. In recent years, the surveillance industry has also been weaponized against student activists organizing against the genocide in <a class="Link" href="https://www.merip.org/2026/04/censorship-and-surveillance-at-us-universities/" target="_blank" >Gaza</a> and the masses protesting U.S. <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/08/13/us/politics/dhs-inquiry-immigration-protests-minnesota.html" target="_blank" >Immigration and Customs Enforcement</a> activity. </p><p>The surveillance culture is now driven by a set of Silicon Valley corporations that have seen their profits soar as our rights are curtailed. Unsurprisingly, their executives have become <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/opinions/interactive/2025/musk-doge-tech-silicon-valley-politics/" target="_blank" >key partners</a> in advancing President Donald Trump’s fascist agenda.</p><p>Palantir, the data-mining firm founded in 2003, received critical initial funding from the <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/andygreenberg/2013/08/14/agent-of-intelligence-how-a-deviant-philosopher-built-palantir-a-cia-funded-data-mining-juggernaut/" target="_blank" >CIA</a> as part of the war on terrorism. The company now has extensive contracts with military and law enforcement agencies around the world, including <a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/ng-interactive/2025/sep/22/ice-palantir-data" target="_blank" >ICE</a>, which uses Palantir data to target immigrants.</p><p>Peter Thiel, Palantir’s co-founder and chairman, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cato-unbound.org/2009/04/13/peter-thiel/education-libertarian/" target="_blank" >wrote</a> in a 2009 essay, “I no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.” </p><p>In more recent times, according to <a class="Link" href="https://www.bloomberg.com/features/2025-peter-thiel-trump-administration-connections/" target="_blank" >Bloomberg</a>, the billionaire tech entrepreneur "used his wealth and influence in Silicon Valley" to help Trump win the presidency and "has deep connections to the new administration’s efforts to remake the government."</p><p>Thiel was also Vice President <a class="Link" href="https://www.forbes.com/sites/antoniopequenoiv/2024/07/16/jd-vance-and-peter-thiel-what-to-know-about-the-relationship-between-trumps-vp-pick-and-the-billionaire/" target="_blank" ><u>JD Vance’s</u></a> mentor and an early financial backer of his political career.</p><p>Thiel isn't alone.</p><h3>Sophisticated spying </h3><p>Google, which went public in 2004, has grown to become a major federal <a class="Link" href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cvgjg98vmzjo" target="_blank" >law enforcement</a> and <a class="Link" href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/google-signs-classified-ai-deal-with-pentagon-information-reports-2026-04-28/" target="_blank" >military</a> contractor. </p><p>Amazon Web Services, Amazon’s cloud computing arm, became a federal contractor with a $600 million <a class="Link" href="https://www.nextgov.com/modernization/2018/04/how-pentagon-contract-sparked-cloud-war/147788/" target="_blank" ><u>intelligence contract</u></a> with the CIA in 2013. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2025/sep/25/microsoft-blocks-israels-use-of-its-technology-in-mass-surveillance-of-palestinians" target="_blank" ><u>Microsoft</u></a> has contracts with the Israeli military and only cut its access to some cloud computing and artificial intelligence after The Guardian revealed Microsoft Azure was being used to conduct mass surveillance of Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza. </p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/02/27/nx-s1-5729118/trump-anthropic-pentagon-openai-ai-weapons-ban" target="_blank" ><u>OpenAI</u></a>, <a class="Link" href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/04/08/anthropic-pentagon-court-ruling-supply-chain-risk.html" target="_blank" ><u>Anthropic</u></a> and other AI firms are all vying for federal contracts. The data centers that suck up water and wreak havoc on energy grids in many communities of color and lower-income neighborhoods exist to support this surveillance regime.</p><p>There is a direct line from the Sept. 11 attacks to the crisis in democracy we are facing today, and it runs through Silicon Valley. The neighbors who dug through our trash in 2001 were a low-tech harbinger for the powered surveillance infrastructure that is being used to suppress peaceful protest and stifle dissent today.</p><p>On the 25th anniversary of Sept. 11, we must reckon with the shameful surveillance-industrial complex it spawned. Americans were told that constant surveillance was the cost of freedom. As Silicon Valley’s grip on our society becomes ironclad, it is clear that sacrificing our freedoms only leads to the further erosion of freedom.</p><p>We must stop Big Tech firms from spying on us and selling our data to repressive state actors trying to take away our freedoms. The only way to ensure democracy for future generations is to rein in the unchecked power of Silicon Valley.</p><p><i>Saqib Bhatti is the executive director of the </i><a class="Link" href="http://acrecampaigns.com/" target="_blank" ><i>Action Center on Race and the Economy</i></a><i> </i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-c50000" name="module-c50000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: I'm 41, afraid to tell woman 35 years older I'm in love
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I'm in love with an older woman. I'm 41, and she is about 35 years older. I have known her since I was a kid. She's the reason I always dated older women. I want to tell her how I feel, but I'm scared she'll be shocked, and I wouldn't want anyone else to find out my feelings, like her kids. I grew up with them.</p><p>We always enjoy our conversations, and I often throw her little hints. When I do, she smiles and likes that I flirt with her, but I've never told her my real feelings. What should I do? — <i>HIDING MY FEELINGS</i></p><p><b>DEAR HIDING:</b> You have nothing to lose by telling her your real feelings. If you do, at the very least she will feel complimented. If there is a possibility that your feelings are reciprocated — well, you are both adults now. If her kids don't object (once they get over the shock), you could have a happy life together. I say this with confidence because years ago a distant cousin of mine married a contemporary of one of her sons.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> What is the proper etiquette when dining out and a hair is found in your meal? I informed the server, and she apologized and gave me credit for a free drink. Others say they wouldn't have eaten the meal and would have requested a new entree. What would you have done? — <i>HAIRY SITUATION</i></p><p><b>DEAR SITUATION:</b> A free drink is not adequate compensation for this unpleasant mistake. When you are presented with food that is inedible for any reason, the manager should be summoned immediately to comp the dish (or more), as well as to offer a sincere apology. When they offer to remake the food, you are within your rights to ask for a different entree. This should allay any suspicion that the kitchen staff might simply pluck out the hair and return the contaminated dish to you.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have a friend in her 80s who always needs to be the center of attention. When someone is talking, not only does she interrupt the speaker, but she also distracts the ones trying to listen by dragging out pictures of her grandchildren.</p><p>She often makes inappropriate sexual comments. She even brought up the subject of sex with my husband! People don't want to be around her. However, she will give the shirt off her back and go out of her way to help anyone. How can I tell her that her conversational style is off-putting without hurting her feelings? — <i>SUFFERING IN SILENCE</i></p><p><b>DEAR SUFFERING:</b> This woman has several bad habits, so don't expect her to correct them all at once. Privately and gently tell her you are not comfortable with her racy comments, nor is your husband. If she begins to show more restraint, be sure to express your sincere appreciation so she feels good about the effort she has made.</p><p>If her bad behavior is a sudden change, it may be a sign of a medical issue. Tell her you have noticed that she hasn't seemed like herself recently and ask if she is keeping up with her medical exams. If you are acquainted with her family, urge them to have her evaluated by her doctor.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: The Ren isn’t shy about artistic risk-taking
entries.summary: <p>The 111-year-old Renaissance Society can’t claim to be the biggest or best-known organization committed to visual arts in Chicago. But this nonprofit, fiercely independent exhibition space on the University of Chicago campus is arguably the most daring and adventurous.</p><p>After taking over as director of the Renaissance Society in 1974, Susanne Ghez put its focus solidly on the art of the present and made it her mission to suss out once new, underrecognized talents such as Isa Genzken and Albert Oehlen. Between 1990 and 2000 alone, 22 artists had their first institutional solo shows in the United States at the Ren.</p><div class="Enhancement FormEnhancement" data-align-center> <div target="_blank" >Privacy Policy</a></p> </div> </form> </bsp-form> </div> </div><p>Today, Myriam Ben Salah, who took over the top post in 2020, continues that tradition of taking risks and championing artists she and her staff believe in. “Of course, risk looks different now than it did in 1975 or 1995,” she said. “The art world is different. Chicago is different. Artists are working differently. But that basic commitment to be early, to be curious and to give artists real authorship – that is something I feel very protective of.”</p><p>Among the many changes in the art world since the 1970s is the proliferation of museums and other spaces that promote contemporary art. But the Ren continues to hold a distinctive place in the Chicago scene and beyond.</p><p>“The Renaissance Society is one of the most important contemporary art institutions in the United States. It’s really a mighty force,” said Ann Goldstein, interim director of the Museum of Contemporary Art, Los Angeles, and former deputy director of the Art Institute of Chicago.</p><p>The Ren’s accomplishments are all the more impressive considering that it has just one gallery — a 40-by-80-foot former lecture hall — and operates with a staff of only nine full- and part-time staff members and a comparatively miniscule annual budget of $2 million with financial support coming mainly from individual and foundation donations and an annual benefit. (Though it functions independently of the university, it does receive space and utilities at no cost.)</p><p>“It has this completely disproportionate reputation relative to its actual physical size,” Ben Salah said.</p><p>The art space’s next presentation, which opens Sept. 12 and runs through Nov. 1, is the American debut of Karimah Ashadu’s “MUSCLE,” a moving-image installation centered on bodybuilders training in the slums of Lagos, Nigeria. In the work, co-commissioned by Ren, the British-born Nigerian artist situates bodybuilding within larger socio-political concerns.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-420000" name="image-420000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a5c1f6e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4096x2299+0+3/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F02%2F8f58546347eb9b2990854ee8b819%2Fkarimah-ashadu-muscle-2025-still-05.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/7c16304/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4096x2299+0+3/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F02%2F8f58546347eb9b2990854ee8b819%2Fkarimah-ashadu-muscle-2025-still-05.jpg 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/047663f/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4096x2299+0+3/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F5f%2F02%2F8f58546347eb9b2990854ee8b819%2Fkarimah-ashadu-muscle-2025-still-05.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Karimah Ashadu, MUSCLE, 2025 [Still], HD digital film, colour with stereo sound, duration: 22 min 20 sec. Courtesy the Artist, Camden Art Centre, Fondazione In Between Art Film, Sadie Coles HQ and The Renaissance Society at the University of Chicago</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ben Salah, 41, grew up in the former French colony of Tunisia speaking Arabic and French and didn’t give any thought to curating, which she didn’t even realize could be a possible career. After high school in Tunis, she moved to France for college, studying theater and humanities. “Then I went to business school, which was a bit of an accident, which I have to say is useful in what I do today,” she said.</p><p>Contemporary art came a little “sideways” into her life in 2009 when she was 24 and started as an intern at the Palais de Tokyo, a prominent contemporary art center in Paris. Her seven-year stint there served as a kind of post-graduate education in contemporary art and curation, which she learned could be an “incredible bridge” between theory and something more tangible and social.</p><p>Like most curators in the field, she had heard of the Ren but had never given any thought to working there. When the position of director and chief curator came open, she was splitting her time between Paris and Los Angeles, where she was working on an exhibition at the Hammer Museum.</p><div Wakaliga Uganda, <i>If Uganda Was America</i>, 2025, Installation View, The Renaissance Society at the University of Chicago. Photo by BOB.</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Ben Salah believes her tenure has been defined in part by making the Ren more “porous” and diversifying the places that its artists come from. As a native of north Africa, she has seen how the art world can ignore certain parts of the world and pigeonhole artists from such places. In spring 2025, the space, for example, presented “If Uganda Was America,” a commissioned film by Wakaliga Uganda, a collective that often produces action movies for as little as $200. This was the group’s first showcase in the United States.</p><p>And in 2022, the Ren presented the final chapter of a film trilogy by Meriem Bennani, who had similar upbringing to that of Ben Salah, growing up in Morocco and later moving to Paris. The two became friends and regular collaborators in 2014 when the curator introduced Bennani’s work in a brief group show at the Palais de Tokyo. “There’s something about a place that has such a history and is rooted in a university context,” Bennani said of the Ren.</p><p>Paulina Pobocha, who became chair and curator of modern and contemporary art at the Art Institute of Chicago in 2024, has been acquainted with Ben Salah for more than five years and knew of her before that. “She was always a curator that I felt was tapped into an art world that extended the beyond geographic boundaries of North America and Europe,” she said, “and that is very much something she has continued to do in her role at the Renaissance Society.”</p><p>Exemplifying Ben Salah’s reach and standing in the art world, she served as curator for the French Pavilion at this year’s edition of the famed Venice Biennale, an international art fair that runs through Nov. 22. The French Ministry of Culture chose Franco-Moroccan artist Yto Barrada for the showcase, and the artist, who serves on the board of the Ren, in turn tapped Ben Salah.</p><p>This year’s Biennale generated an uproar over the inclusion of Russian and Israeli national pavilions, with the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/2026/04/30/arts/design/israel-artist-venice-biennale.html" target="_blank" ><u>entire awards jury resigning</u></a> before the opening. “A lot of things are controversial these days,” said Ben Salah, who is returning to the Biennale in October with a group of Ren board members. “The world is in shambles, and art exists within that world, so obviously it is affected by everything that goes on around it. The Biennale is no exception.”</p>

entries.title: Independent governor candidate Collin Corbett aims to give voters ‘a home again’ in polarized Illinois
entries.summary: <p>It’s deja vu from 2022 at the top of the ticket in this November’s race for Illinois governor, but there is one new face trying to shape the conversation.</p><p>Independent candidate Collin Corbett says he’s providing the middle ground many voters yearn for between incumbent Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker and Republican nominee Darren Bailey, who lost soundly four years ago on a hardline conservative platform.</p><p>While Pritzker attacks Bailey for his <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/19/chris-welch-state-fair-illinois-house-sexual-harassment-harry-benton" target="_blank" ><u>allegiance to President Donald Trump</u></a> and the downstate farmer returns fire on the billionaire governor’s progressive agenda, Corbett’s looking for “a space for people to be able to go where they can have a home again in our politics.”</p><p>“As both parties have continued to chase the extremes, both ideologically and on a personality level, more and more people feel like they don't have a home,” said Corbett, a 40-year-old political consultant from Palatine. “Being able to give them a place where we can talk common sense on policies, we can identify the challenges and actually seek out solutions while the two parties just continue to snip at each other — we can go and try to make things better in our state.”</p><p>A fiscal conservative who supports abortion rights and opposes much of the Trump agenda, Corbett collected 37,000 signatures to get on the ballot and has pumped $500,000 into a campaign with twice the spending power of Bailey’s two months out of the Nov. 3 election.</p><p>Corbett, who won’t match the wealthy Pritzker’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2026/08/17/gov-jb-pritzker-pours-65m-into-his-campaign-fund-ahead-of-november-elections" target="_blank" ><u>bottomless resources</u></a>, took leave from his consulting firm and his podcast earlier this year while leaving the Republican Party altogether, abandoning “a political process that's actively hurting people.” He pointed to Trump’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bearing-the-blitz/2026/09/03/operation-midway-blitz-deportation-toll-angela-sedeno-cindy-eigler-vero-ortiz-immigrants" target="_blank" ><u>aggressive deportation campaign</u></a>.</p><p>“I've spoken out a lot about immigration, obviously, where your political position is hurting people, hurting communities. And then you get to Minneapolis — literally killing people,” said Corbett, who has long “actively opposed Trump when he's wrong.”</p><p>“But I also believe he's in the White House. He's the president, so when he's right, you should work with him and support him,” said Corbett, who started out working on the campaigns of former suburban GOP stalwarts and U.S. Reps. Peter Roskam and Bob Dold.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-f70000" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/03/17/governor-illinois-republican-race-primary-results" target="_blank" ><u>Bailey</u></a>, Corbett argues Pritzker — who has done little to quell speculation on a 2028 presidential run — could better serve the state by establishing a working relationship with Trump.</p><p>“[Pritzker’s] presidential ambitions are not good for Illinoisans because he's going to oppose Trump no matter what, because he wants to be president,” Corbett said. “I understand why he's doing it, but it's leading to this petty feud between Trump and Pritzker, where two ego-driven, very petty individuals are trying to hurt the other side.</p><p>“Everyday people are getting hurt as a result — Trump yanking funding from mental health services and child care services. This is hurting real people, and then you see what happened with ICE coming into Chicago and targeting our state,” he said.</p><p>Following Illinois’ 12th <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/illinois-governor/2026/09/02/back-to-back-fiscal-upgrades-illinois-jbpritzker-re-election-bid-darren-bailey" target="_blank" ><u>credit rating upgrade</u></a> under Pritzker, Corbett argues “JB gets a bit of a pass because he has done some things better than his predecessors.”</p><p>“You can only grade on a curve for so long," Corbett said. “A lot of people, even left of center, have said structurally, there are changes we need to make in this state, because this is not sustainable. I think their hearts are in the right place, but when you have a state that isn't growing, you're not generating that revenue.”</p><p>A Pritzker campaign spokesperson said, “Donald Trump is an existential threat to our democracy, and defending Illinois means standing up to Trump. Gov. Pritzker is proud to be on the front lines of that fight while also restoring fiscal responsibility, making historic investments in education, and lowering costs for working families.”</p><p>On the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/springfield/2026/08/20/darren-bailey-illinois-republicans-state-fair-pritzker" target="_blank" ><u>other end of the spectrum</u></a>, “Bailey's approach of just slashing government to the bone is not going to work, nor is it feasible,” Corbett said.</p><p>“[Bailey’s] campaign is all about telling people what they want to hear instead of actually presenting solutions to the problems that we face… I know it gets me fewer likes on social media, but I don't care.”</p><p>A Bailey campaign spokesperson called Corbett "a failed political consultant who has spent his career helping politicians raise taxes on working families. Now he wants voters to believe he’ll fight for them. The reality is simple: a vote for Collin is a vote for JB Pritzker and more of the same failed policies costing Illinois families dearly."</p><p>As a political consultant, Corbett knows the odds are stacked against an independent, though he says his polling shows he’d do better in a head-to-head matchup with Pritzker than Bailey would.</p><p>Corbett says his campaign is more about building a bridge away from two-party tribalism.</p><p>“There is a lot of hope for our movement beyond my run for governor, a lot of hope that we can create a space where people can lead in their communities, even if that's somebody who isn't on the far end of the spectrum on either the right or the left,” he said. “We need that because there's a lot of really good people who want to step up and lead in the state.”</p>
