entries.title: 'Orbital' is the 2026 One Book, One Chicago selection
entries.summary: <p>The Chicago Public Library is looking to outer space for this year's citywide read. Samantha Harvey's “Orbital” will be this year's <a class="Link" href="https://www.chipublib.org/one-book-one-chicago/" target="_blank" ><u>One Book, One Chicago</u></a> selection, the library announced Wednesday.</p><p>The slim celestial novel won the 2024 Booker Prize (an annual literary award that goes to a single work of fiction published in the U.K. or Ireland). class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Chicago Public Library Commissioner Chris Brown said with this year’s One Book, One Chicago selection is meant to “remind people of our shared commonality.”</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Anthony Vazquez/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>As the library’s annual program turns 25, this year's One Book, One Chicago program will also feature a children's book for the first time. That selection is Oliver Jeffers’ picture book, “Here We Are: Notes for Living on Planet Earth,” which will be featured in story times at branches across the city and available for parents to check out to read at home.</p><p>There is also a selection aimed at middle-grade readers, “The Lion of Mars” by author Jennifer L. Holm.</p><p>In total, Brown said the multiple selections around a single theme are an attempt to connect readers across all ages. “We're wanting to make One Book, One Chicago an experience for all Chicagoans, thinking about our city intergenerationally,” Brown said.</p><p>The program began in 2001 with Harper Lee’s American classic “To Kill a Mockingbird.” In recent years, selections have included “<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/books/2025/09/03/chicago-public-library-2025-one-book-olga-dies-dreaming-xochitl-gonzalez" target="_blank" ><u>Olga Dies Dreaming</u></a>,” “<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/books/2024/09/04/tomorrow-and-tomorrow-and-tomorrow-one-book-one-chicago-2024" target="_blank" ><u>Tomorrow, and Tomorrow, and Tomorrow</u></a>” and “<a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/culture-the-arts/2023/09/06/there-there-is-the-2023-one-book-one-chicago-pick" target="_blank" ><u>There There</u></a>.”</p><p>The book is selected by a committee of people, including library staff and representatives from local museums, universities and cultural organizations.</p><p>This year, the library system will partner with the Adler Planetarium on a series of events around the book. The lineup also includes showings of space-related films from “Apollo 13” to “Hidden Figures” and “Project Hail Mary” at various library branches throughout the fall.</p><p>Other planned programs include a silent reading soiree at the Harold Washington Library from 5-7 p.m. on Sept. 23 and a screening of the documentary “Operation Space Station,” followed by a community discussion, at 5:30 p.m. on Oct. 8 at Harold Washington.</p><p>Harvey will appear virtually at a keynote event on Nov. 19, in conversation with Booklist magazine’s Editor, Donna Seaman.</p><p>Brown said the library’s goal is to take the experience beyond a shared read to real-world connections, “where you're getting to be with other Chicagoans who are excited about the book and excited to experience themes outside and beyond the book.”</p><p>As part of the One Book program, the library system will have nearly 1,000 copies of “Orbital” in circulation, including copies in Chinese, Polish, Spanish and Korean.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-040000" name="image-040000"></a> <picture data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a6e1d5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fa2%2F3b69ba6b41dcaed8b3c1fe0550cd%2Fap24317820995589.jpg" " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a6e1d5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fa2%2F3b69ba6b41dcaed8b3c1fe0550cd%2Fap24317820995589.jpg 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/c803568/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fa2%2F3b69ba6b41dcaed8b3c1fe0550cd%2Fap24317820995589.jpg 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/a6e1d5c/2147483647/strip/true/crop/6000x3367+0+316/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F91%2Fa2%2F3b69ba6b41dcaed8b3c1fe0550cd%2Fap24317820995589.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Samantha Harvey after winning the 2024 Booker Prize for her novel, “Orbital,” which has been selected as Chicago’s citywide read this fall.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Alberto Pezzali/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In Harvey’s book, as the astronauts look down on Earth, they grapple with climate change and wonder, “Will robots take our jobs?” Just as in real life, the fictional astronauts are aware that their station — like the current iteration of the real-world International Space Station — is coming to an end. After more than 25 years of continuous human presence aboard the station, the ISS is <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2024/02/21/1232639289/international-space-station-retirement-space-stations-future" target="_blank" ><u>set to be decommissioned in 2030</u></a>. </p><p>The end of this era of space exploration is part of what motivated Harvey to write the book, she said in an interview for <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bZ8brVxtgXc" target="_blank" ><u>The Late Show with Stephen Colbert</u></a>’s book club.</p><p>“I could see the peace project that is the ISS is coming to an end,” Harvey said. “For me, it was always a book that was about looking with some degree of nostalgia at the passing of that era, and the fact that we are moving into something quite different.”</p><p>While Harvey herself is not an astronaut, she writes with commanding authority about what it's like to be cooped up in space for a long period of time with a group of people from around the world.</p><p>Brown said it's that message of unity that he hopes resonates with Chicagoans.</p><p>“Chicago is such a diverse city. We have so many different vantage points, so many different lived experiences,” Brown said. “I think having a book where you can see these characters from different representative parts of the world, but have that shared kind of vantage point. I think there's something that we can gain from that in Chicago.”</p><p><i>Courtney Kueppers is an arts and culture reporter at WBEZ. </i></p>

entries.title: Plantasia at Garfield Park Conservatory embraces its roots as a celebration of ambient and electronic music
entries.summary: <p>Plantasia is the one time every year when the greenhouse turns into a house party. Held at Garfield Park Conservatory Sept. 10-11, it’s a two-day celebration of ambient and electronic music set among palm trees and succulents that some believe is just as much for people as it is for the plants.</p><p>“I do believe plants have certain receptors to vibration,” said performer Makaya McCraven, "and communication through vibration and connection is part of the intangibles of sound and music.”</p><p>The local jazz luminary will headline the final day of Plantasia, which is now in its eighth year. But the roots of the event and this intersection between music and horticulture actually go back decades to an album celebrating its 50th anniversary this year.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Makaya McCraven</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Itzi Marques</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 1976, composer Mort Garson wanted to test a growing theory that suggested plants needed more than good soil and water to grow — they needed good music too. Armed with a Moog synthesizer and a range of test subjects in his house, Garson got to work and created the album, “Mother Earth’s Plantasia: Warm earth music for plants…and the people that love them.”</p><p> It really should’ve been a blip of an album; at first, the only copies available came with the purchase of a houseplant at the Mother Earth store in Los Angeles. But over time, as the record gained considerable respect as a pioneer in the electronic space, it became a cult classic that was increasingly hard to find.</p><p>That was until 2018, when the indie label Sacred Bones in Brooklyn, New York, got the rights to reissue Garson’s masterpiece — and when news reached the Empty Bottle Presents team, they knew they had to do something. </p><p>“Coincidentally, we had just been in touch with the Conservatory about doing events there … and when we heard about Sacred Bones making the album available on vinyl again, I reached out and was like, ‘hey, we have access to this incredible space. Wouldn't it be rad to do a version of the record with live performances in this beautiful setting?’” recalls Brent Heyl, director of music at 16” on Center, the parent group behind the Bottle, Salt Shed, Thalia Hall and SPACE.</p><p>While the first year of Plantasia was wholly devoted to recreating Garson’s soundscape, the program has since expanded to welcome ambient and experimental artists of all flavors performing original works. Music acts are co-curated by Sacred Bones, which continues to be involved in the event, and a part of the proceeds also benefits the Garson estate in homage to its namesake. </p><p>This year’s edition features Thursday night headliner Helado Negro and Reyna Tropical, who just released a collaborative new album this summer. “They’re two artists that have incredible history with us, and it will be cool to see what they have going on together,” Heyl said. And tapping McCraven to close out night two, Heyl added, was meant to be "such a nice way to showcase him in the city where he's from.”</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-380000" name="module-380000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Plantasia</h3><br><b>When:</b> 5:30 p.m., Sept. 10-11<br><b>Where:</b> Garfield Park Conservatory, 300 N Central Park Ave.<br><b>Tickets:</b> $55 for one-day pass, $95 for two-day pass<br><b>Info:</b> emptybottle.com</div> </div><p>Other highlights across the two days include a rare appearance from Italian composer Gigi Masin, a four-hour set from Japanese electronic whiz Chee Shimizu in the conservatory’s Fern Room and Welsh guitarist Gwenifer Raymond.<b> </b></p><p>“She might not be people's first thought for a Plantasia set because she's a shredding acoustic guitar player, but it’s really beautiful stuff,” Heyl said. “I think she will offer a nice break in the sonic flow from electronics.” </p><p>In addition to the music acts, there’s also a public tape swap in the Children's Garden hosted by StretchMetal and DJ sets from the staff of Bucktown’s Torn Light Records. “They have the deepest collection of leftfield jazz, experimental and ambient music. Their collection of cassette tapes and books is like few I've ever seen, and they seem really tapped into what it is that we're presenting here,” Heyl said.<b> </b>And for anyone who wants to remember the event for posterity, a 2026 poster will be for sale, designed by A. Savage, the lead singer of Parquet Courts who has performed at Plantasia in the past. </p><p>Someone who is new to the event this year, however, is McCraven, who is also keen to explore how a unique space, like a conservatory, can shape music performances. It’s a relationship he focused on for his latest release, 2025’s “Off the Record," a compilation of four individual EPs driven by moments of improvisation in distinct settings. Among them was the time he was artist-in-residence at Winter Jazz Fest in 2025 and an appearance at Brooklyn’s Public Records that same year to celebrate the 10th anniversary of his album “In The Moment” as well as McCraven’s Tuesday night residency at The Hideout in 2017.</p><p>“I wanted to keep the integrity of each space we were in, and the cast of people I created with in those spaces,” says McCraven. “The environment and being in the moment are important to color everything I do. … There are possibilities in each and every room.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Plantasia transforms Garfield Park Conservatory into a house party every September.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Scott Teresi</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Empty Bottle Presents has a similar philosophy when considering spaces where performances are held. Talent bookers have looked beyond the confines of traditional venues to hold shows, whether it’s the Garfield Park Conservatory or spots like Bohemian National Cemetery and the Rockefeller Memorial Chapel at the University of Chicago.</p><p>“We want to give people a different way to experience music,” Heyl said. “I love our venues, and I think they each have a purpose for a very specific type of experience. But if you go to a lot of shows, you can kind of feel like you’re just returning to the same place over and over again. Being able to present these bands in new settings makes you appreciate them in different ways.”</p><p>Of the whole EBP portfolio, Heyl particularly loves Plantasia for a reason Garson would appreciate, too. </p><p>“It’s surrounded by so much nature … and it’s nice to just feel the vibrations of the sounds and connection to the world. If you let yourself drift away, it’s a beautiful thing.”</p>

entries.title: With Ald. Rodriguez not seeking re-election, Johnson loses key City Council ally
entries.summary: <p>Mayor Brandon Johnson is losing one of his staunchest City Council allies.</p><p>Ald. Mike Rodriguez (22nd), the Workforce Development Committee chair who helped Johnson deliver two of the proudest accomplishments on his progressive to-do list, has decided not to seek re-election.</p><p>“My daughter’s entering high school. I’ve got four years left with that beautiful baby. I’ve got an ailing father. I’ve got a chess champion son… It’s the right time for me” to step back, said Rodriguez, who all but endorsed 10th police district council member Elianne Bahena as his replacement.</p><p>“I was at a soccer tournament in Minnesota with my son in July… And I remember having to walk away from the cheering crowd because I wanted City Council members to hear my `aye’ [vote] in a committee meeting… Half the trip, my wife was telling my kids to be quiet because I had calls for work… I want to be present for my family. “</p><p>Rodriguez, 48, is the second veteran alderperson to choose political retirement over a re-election bid. Ald. Marty Quinn (13th), one of Johnson’s most outspoken critics, is <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/fran-spielman-show/2026/07/08/one-of-mayor-brandon-johnson-most-ardent-city-council-adversaries-wont-seek-reelection-in-2027" >also leaving the City Council.</a></p><p>A protege of retiring U.S. Rep. Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, Rodriguez has spent his two terms on the City Council positioning himself as a champion for working people. He was the chief co-sponsor of a Fair Workweek Ordinance that advanced key protections for employees facing unpredictable schedules.</p><p>He championed another important protection for Chicago workers through the Paid Leave Ordinance that granted employees a minimum of ten paid days off. For Rodriguez, those accomplishments were more personal than political.</p><p>The motivation dates back to his childhood. He recalled that his mother was able to take him, his brother and sister to Taste of Chicago — with a Home Run Inn pizza and a boat ride in between — because she was a union worker who had paid time off.</p><p>“I think about how many Chicagoans can’t even take a day off to stay with their kid home from school if they’re sick — can’t help an ailing mother or father if they need to be there,” Rodriguez told the Sun-Times.</p><p>“That’s why I was so proud to be the champion and pass the most expansive paid leave policy in the country… The first two years of this administration, I’ll put my record as workforce development chair against anybody else’s in the history of the city.”</p><p>Both accomplishments on Johnson’s progressive to-do-list were achieved early in the mayor’s administration. But it’s been downhill from there.</p><p>Johnson used his third veto to preserve another key promise on his progressive agenda — eliminating the sub-minimum wage for tipped workers — and managed to make it stick.</p><p>But an emboldened City Council then froze the hourly pay of tipped workers at 76% of the minimum wage for the next two years for large restaurants, and for four more years for smaller establishments.</p><p>After renegade alderpersons rejected the mayor's corporate head tax and approved an alternative city budget that legalized video gambling terminals, Johnson joined forces with Bally’s in lobbying for a repeal that Rodriguez expects to fail.</p><p>“It was the strangest thing to do to undercut Bally’s... They give us $4 million annually. But I’m also dealing in political reality. That side won with their vote… Video gaming’s here," he said.</p><p>Rodriguez acknowledged that the “struggle to stand up for working people” continues and will not be “solved in this mayoral administration or even the next.” But he hopes to join his Southwest Side colleague, Ald. Julia Ramirez (12th) in passing protections for warehouse workers before leaving office in May.</p><p>Rodriguez's tenure included Hilco’s botched smokestack implosion at the former Crawford coal generating station and Operation Midway Blitz, which menaced residents of Little Village a year ago. At one point, members of Rodriguez's own aldermanic staff were swept off the streets.</p><p>Rodriguez said he won't forget standing on the corner of 26th and Pulaski watching now-former U.S. Border Patrol chief Greg Bovino and his agents take a left turn down 26th Street and snatch a man in front of a six-year-old boy.</p><p>“This kid witnessed a person being taken indiscriminately because they were brown-skinned. What I saw was the devil in Bovino. I looked him eye to eye,” Rodriguez said.</p><p>“I get a flash grenade at my foot. That smoke from that grenade filled the car of the child who was sitting there. I remember seeing that child devastated, crying, not knowing what the heck was going on. I just think about this being a core memory for that child for the rest of his life.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-e50000" name="html-embed-module-e50000"></a><iframe allow="monetization" frameborder="0" height="200" scrolling="no" src="https://play.prx.org/e?ge=prx_12963_3b7ec6b9-ff6a-4216-96cf-5f8322c705c1&uf=https%3A%2F%2Fpublicfeeds.net%2Ff%2F12963%2Ffeed-rss.xml" style="min-width: 300px;" width="100%"></iframe> </div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Why one Chicago motel encouraged guests to smash stuff in the 1960s
entries.summary: <p>Brandee Neal holds a baseball bat at the Angry Cactus Lounge on Chicago’s North Side. She’s facing down an array of old consumer electronics inside one of its four concrete-walled “rage rooms.” Neal wears protective gear, including a face shield and an apron, while her friend records a video. Then she starts whaling on an old computer monitor and does not stop for half a minute.</p><p>“It was an outlet that I didn’t know I needed,” Neal says afterward. The experience is equal parts therapy and entertainment: “I’m in therapy, but […] you can’t punch your therapist in the face.”</p><p>Rage rooms are a popular sector these days. More than 500 dot the United States, according to the <a class="Link" href="https://rageroomly.com/rage-room-statistics-in-the-usa/" target="_blank" ><u>Rage Room Alliance</u></a>, and many of them trace their roots to a Tokyo pop-up called the Venting Place, which appeared during the Great Recession around 2008. But Chicago may actually have a claim to the world’s very first rage room, nearly 50 years earlier.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>A rage room at the Angry Cactus Lounge, 2525 N. Elston Ave., is piled with smashed electronics.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Justin Bull/WBEZ</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>In 1962, the Imperial Inn opened at Canal and Harrison streets in Downtown Chicago. To attract guests, it offered a space in the basement where patrons could release their anger by throwing breakable items at the wall: the Frustration Room.</p><p>“You would come in and there would be this sort of counter before you,” said Paul Durica, director of curation and exhibitions at the Chicago History Museum. “It would be laid out with all of these different household objects — lamps, plates, bowls, light bulbs — and in front of you would be basically a steel-plated wall, and you were encouraged just to kind of let loose and throw things at the wall.”</p><p>Who thought this place up and why did it disappear? Curious City looked into the Frustration Room’s origins and found its emergence coincided with a changing domestic travel landscape.</p><h3><b>The Frustration Room</b></h3><p>The idea of putting a gimmick like a rage room inside a hotel or motel is not as far afield as one might assume, according to Mark E. Young, hotel historian and director of the Hospitality Industry Archive at the Hilton College University of Houston.</p><p>“To me, the best gimmick ever is the DoubleTree chocolate chip cookie,” a treat which has greeted guests at the hotel chain since 1986, Young said.</p><p>Like a swimming pool or a spa or a continental breakfast, the Frustration Room was an incentive to get bodies in beds. Young said the emergence of America’s new interstate highway system in the mid-20th century led to a particularly fierce period of competition.</p><p>“All the downtowns and all of the American cities were very quickly trying to figure out how they could make it easier for the people traveling by car to get to their downtown hotel, because people weren’t traveling by train anymore,” he said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-ec0000" name="image-ec0000"></a> <picture class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Edward Rebbe of Skokie, Illinois, relaxing in the Frustration Room of the Imperial Inn at Harrison and Canal in Chicago, July 13, 1962. After driving all day and seeing stop signs etc., he can come into the Frustration Room and smash dishes and light bulbs to release stress. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>ST-17654953, Chicago Sun-Times collection, Chicago History Museum</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>The Frustration Room was originally decorated with traffic signs and marketed at drivers who were frustrated by this new standard of getting around.</p><p>“Even today in the 21st century, driving is deeply frustrating,” Durica said. “So, on the one hand, it’s a gimmick, but on the other hand, it seems to be recognizing a real sort of psychic need.”</p><p>If your frustrations ran deeper than the traffic, the Imperial Inn offered a variety of other targets. Visitors could throw a lamp at a photograph of President John F. Kennedy, Republican Sen. Barry Goldwater or Premier Nikita Khrushchev, the leader of the Soviet Union.</p><p>“The [Imperial] Inn really wanted to attract tourists, and it really wanted to attract people coming to the city for conventions,” Durica said. “[The Frustration Room] was just another selling point.”</p><p>The Imperial Inn also advertised an in-house psychiatrist, a service aimed at stressed-out executives and weary businessmen, according to one article in the San Francisco Examiner. “After all, there’s a couch in every room,” the Imperial Inn’s general manager said.</p><div class="Enhancement" Star and even Time magazine.</p><p>Local journalists checked it out too. also an inventor of unsuccessful products, including a horizontal refrigerator and a wall-to-wall mattress.</p><p>During the publicity campaign surrounding the Frustration Room, he attempted to bring the gag to Florida. An article in the Miami News on July 23, 1962, claimed that Linsky copyrighted the idea for the Frustration Room and was making it available to other businesses.</p><h3><b>“Despite all my rage”</b></h3><p>The Imperial Inn became a Ramada Inn in the late 1960s. Today, it’s a Holiday Inn & Suites, and there’s no accompanying rage room, according to the general manager.</p><p>It’s unclear when exactly the Frustration Room was no longer a place people could visit to smash their blues away. Advertisements for “the world’s only Frustration Room” appeared in newspapers and hotel reference books until at least 1966. At least one customer recalls visiting as late as 1970. But the Imperial Inn had other problems.</p><p>“It seems like the Imperial Inn had a very challenging sort of run,” Durica said. “They’re very clearly desperate and keen on getting people in.”</p><div A Chicago Tribune exposé pointed to the business taking questionable loans from the Teamsters union in the mid-1960s, and Durica also found evidence of police gambling raids there in the same timeframe.</p><p>“By the late 1960s, it’s not the Imperial Inn anymore. It's the Ramada,” Durica said. “And at that point, is there a Frustration Room? I don’t know. It just kind of vanishes from the record.”</p><p>Though the Frustration Room is gone, it has plenty of next of kin. Chicago and the suburbs have <a class="Link" href="https://www.angrycactuslounge.com/" target="_blank" ><u>rage room businesses</u></a> on offer, and the <a class="Link" href="https://www.thescreamclub.com/" target="_blank" ><u>Chicago Scream Club</u></a> meets on summer Sunday nights at the North Avenue Beach pier.</p><p>Experts — including Dr. Sheila Dowd, associate director at the Center for Anxiety and Traumatic Stress at Rush University Medical Center in Chicago — warn against using rage rooms as a replacement for therapy.</p><p>“That experience is very momentary. entries.title: 3 stabbed in 2 separate domestic fights in Rogers Park
entries.summary: <p>Two men and a woman were recovering in good condition at St. Francis Hospital in Evanston after two separate stabbings early Wednesday in the Rogers Park neighborhood. </p><p>Most recently, about 3:50 a.m. a man and woman, 20 and 29 were inside a home in the 7400 block of North Wolcott Avenue when a woman they knew entered and she allegedly stabbed the two during a fight, officials said.</p><p>The woman was stabbed in the chest and the man suffered cuts to his right forearm, police said. Both were taken to St. Francis in good condition.</p><p>About three hours earlier, around 12:50 a.m., a 26-year-old man was arguing with a woman inside a home in the 7600 block of North Bosworth Avenue, Chicago police said. </p><p>The woman stabbed the man in the forearm with a sharp object and fled the scene, police said. He was also taken to St. Francis where he was in good condition. </p><p>Both attacks appear to be domestic and police classified them as two separate incidents. </p>

entries.title: 2-alarm fire leaves West Town apartment residents displaced
entries.summary: <p>No one was hurt but several people were displaced after an extra alarm blaze tore through a West Town apartment building early Wednesday. </p><p>Fire officials responded to the fire around 2:40 a.m. in the 1400 block of West Grand Avenue and it elevated to a two-alarm fire roughly 20 minutes later, according to the Chicago Fire Department. The fire was eventually extinguished just after 4:30 a.m. </p><p>No injuries were reported but the Red Cross was called to assist with displacements, though fire officials don’t know exactly how many residents were impacted. </p><p>The cause of the fire was under investigation. </p>
entries.author: Sun-Times Wire

entries.title: Lincoln-Way East students walk out after classmates, coach caught making racist comments
entries.summary: <p>Dozens of students walked out of Lincoln-Way East High School in south suburban Frankfort Wednesday morning after two allegations surfaced that their classmates and on of their coaches made racist comments toward students at another school.</p><p>The mood was somber and the halls were nearly empty ahead of the demonstration. But the students who remained said they were determined to make their voices heard.</p><p>“We want to let people know that Lincoln-Way East is not just a predominantly white school that's full of racist people,” said 14-year-old Teniola Omokaye. “There's a big demographic of black people that go here and we actually stand for something.”</p><p>Student organizers <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racial-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >planned the walkout</a> to stand with Homewood-Flossmoor High School and send a message that the behavior does not represent the broader Lincoln-Way East student body.</p><p>The first incident occurred at Friday’s football game in Flossmoor, where Lincoln-Way East students were caught on video racially taunting the Homewood-Flossmoor student section by mimicking monkeys.</p><p></p><p>The next morning, Homewood-Flossmoor officials said a coach and members of Lincoln-Way East’s girls cross-country team taunted the H-F team during a meet in Western Springs.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >Second racist Lincoln-Way East incident alleged by Homewood-Flossmoor</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Lincoln-Way East acknowledged what happened at Friday’s football game and apologized. The Lincoln-Way School District, however, denied the allegations involving the girls cross-country team in a statement issued Tuesday afternoon.</p><p>Homewood-Flossmoor said it plans to pursue legal action on both incidents.</p>
entries.author: Cindy Hernandez

entries.title: After alleged racism, Homewood-Flossmoor weighs future with Lincoln-Way East
entries.summary: <p>Last weekend’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-sports/2026/09/08/lincoln-way-east-racist-incident-homewood-flossmoor" >racial incidents between Lincoln-Way East and Homewood-Flossmoor</a> have brought future athletic events between the schools into question.</p><p>The Lincoln-Way East freshman football team did not play at H-F on Saturday morning after the racial harassment incident at the varsity football game Friday night. The schools made the decision together after a phone conversation between Lincoln-Way Supt. Scott Tingley and H-F Supt. Jennifer Norrell.</p><p>“Tensions were high,” Norrell told the Sun-Times. “We agreed it was better to just spend our day doing more investigations and getting a handle on what happened Friday night. I don’t think either one of us had a good grasp of what was going on.”</p><p>Later in the weekend, Homewood-Flossmoor officials accused a Lincoln-Way East girls cross country coach and team members of racial abuse.</p><p>H-F provided written statements from three cross country athletes describing a Lincoln-Way East coach making comments about “running past those monkeys,” and that some of the Lincoln-Way East team began cheering and making “noises that were racist” and “monkey gestures.”</p><p>Lincoln-Way investigated the incident and concluded that “neither its staff nor student athletes intended to harass, intimidate or offend any of their competitors or those competitors’ families.”</p><p>Norrell is disappointed in Lincoln-Way’s response to the cross country incident.</p><p>“We don’t have to see things from the same political views,” Norrell said. “But common, decent respect for other humans is something, certainly as adults, we can have. How can we continue to be upset with the actions of children when we don’t have adults that will stand up and do the right thing?”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-portrait-right> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-c20000" name="image-c20000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium-3x4"> <source type="image/webp" width="375" height="500" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/e49d335/2147483647/strip/true/crop/192x256+32+0/resize/375x500!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F9f%2F94c77c7a44d2806046eb0a97fd20%2Fdrjennifernorrell-copy.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="375" height="500" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5054d6b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/192x256+32+0/resize/375x500!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F9f%2F94c77c7a44d2806046eb0a97fd20%2Fdrjennifernorrell-copy.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Homewood-Flossmoor Supt. Jennifer Norrell" width="375" height="500" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/5054d6b/2147483647/strip/true/crop/192x256+32+0/resize/375x500!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Ff0%2F9f%2F94c77c7a44d2806046eb0a97fd20%2Fdrjennifernorrell-copy.jpg" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSI1MDBweCIgd2lkdGg9IjM3NXB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Homewood-Flossmoor Supt. Jennifer Norrell</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Homewood-Flossmoor High School</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Homewood-Flossmoor has a varsity girls tennis match scheduled at Lincoln-Way East on Sept. 12, a golf meet with Lincoln-Way East at Green Garden Country Club on Sept. 14, and a boys varsity soccer match against Lincoln-Way East at Homewood-Flossmoor on Sept. 16. Both schools are members of the Southwest Suburban Conference.</p><p>“I already had kids ask, 'Are we going to be ok?” Norrell said. “I don’t want my varsity tennis team to have to forfeit an invitational. But I also know that there is some level of fear. What I have told them is at the end of the day, if this is still going on and we don’t have a way out of this that won’t jeopardize our record, I’m going to ride on the bus. I’m going to go with them and sit next to them the entire match. I don’t have anything else we can do. I’m just going to be present and make sure the kids don’t feel unsafe.”</p><p>Both of Homewood-Flossmoor’s recent public statements on the incidents mentioned possible legal action against Lincoln-Way East. That is still on the table.</p><p>“Right now our board of education attorney is weighing all the options and trying to make a determination,” Norrell said. “They have not decided on a path.”</p><p>Norrell has spoken with several local politicians since Friday's incident.</p><p>“They want to know how we mend this,” Norrell said. “Our communities are very close. One of the things I told them is that we take our lead from the young people.”</p><p>Around 40 Lincoln-Way East students held a school walkout in protest of the racial incidents on Wednesday.</p><p>“Our [H-F] students view that as support, hands down,” Norrell said. “They felt supported. We appreciate that they are doing it to show that they too believe it was wrong.”</p><p>On Wednesday, the Illinois High School Association told the Sun-Times that scheduling issues between the schools would be part of their conversations with each school, but they don’t typically have much involvement in regular-season scheduling.</p><p>Lincoln-Way East and Lincoln Way School District did not respond to requests for interviews.</p>

entries.title: Kiss-cam video serves as backdrop to raucous public meeting in Lyons Township
entries.summary: <p>The kiss-cam saga continued this week in Lyons Township as the elected board held its first public meeting since footage from surveillance cameras surfaced showing one official getting smooched by a suburban mayor after hours at the township’s Countryside offices.</p><p>But much of the drama at the Tuesday night board meeting centered not on the kisser or who he was kissing, but a third political figure who had been accused of playing a part in leaking the video that showed the embarrassing encounter. </p><p>Chris Getty is the Lyons Township supervisor, essentially the top administrator for that obscure public agency that handles, among other things, social services for a cluster of western suburbs that make up the jurisdiction.</p><p>Getty is also the mayor of the village of Lyons, part of the township, and a candidate running as an independent for Congress.</p><p>Getty is not exactly a political pal of Lyons Township Clerk Elyse Hoffenberg, who is running as a Democrat for Cook County Board and was captured on video getting kissed in July by Bridgeview Mayor Steve Landek, who is the township’s Democratic committeeman and a former state senator.</p><p>Hoffenberg, who is married to someone else, initially told Patch the kiss was inappropriate and that Landek had apologized to her. Later, she described the kiss “as a lighthearted, friendly and non-romantic moment among colleagues.”</p><p>The surveillance cameras had been installed in the offices at Hoffenberg’s request as a security measure, officials said.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-a60000" name="image-a60000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1aa73f1/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F37%2F0f1c3f4e4a04bdc3bdaf496c61be%2Fimg-0622-2.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/681f400/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F37%2F0f1c3f4e4a04bdc3bdaf496c61be%2Fimg-0622-2.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/251ba99/2147483647/strip/true/crop/4032x2263+0+381/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2Fe4%2F37%2F0f1c3f4e4a04bdc3bdaf496c61be%2Fimg-0622-2.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Lyons Township Clerk Elyse Hoffenberg, facing forward, is shown at the Lyons Township board meeting Tuesday night. Township Supervisor Chris Getty is shown back left.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Robert Herguth / Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Not long after the incident, Hoffenberg’s Republican opponent in the county board race, Liz Gorman, got wind of the video and submitted an open-records request for a copy — prompting Hoffenberg to accuse Getty of involvement in the tip-off and of potentially deleting images.</p><p>But on Tuesday night, Getty insisted that he had nothing to do with the situation, reading from a prepared statement that said:</p><p>“The recent accusations... are completely false and without merit. The Clerk has chosen to manufacture procedural drama, promote baseless conspiracy theories, and launch political attacks against my office and the dedicated professionals who serve our township.</p><p>“The residents of Lyons Township expect and deserve the highest standards of professionalism and integrity from their elected leadership.”</p><p>Hoffenberg also initially accused Gorman of dirty politics, saying: “My political opponents attempted to extort me regarding this video, saying they would drop their threats to release it if I end my campaign. I am certain that our community will find this kind of old school politics of harassment abhorrent, and I won’t be bullied.”</p><p>Gorman attended Tuesday’s meeting and spoke during the public comment entries.title: White Sox beat Cubs 56-48, in Chicago ballpark arrests in recent years
entries.summary: <p>Chicago baseball fans have been packing Wrigley and Rate fields this year as the Cubs and White Sox push for the playoffs.</p><p>But in some cases, the action on the field has been overshadowed by the hijinks in the stands. </p><p>Star Cubs center fielder Pete Crow-Armstrong had <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/05/18/cubs-pete-crow-armstrong-heckler-white-sox-fan-crosstown-rivalry-viral" target="_blank" >a heated exchange with a female White Sox fan</a> during a Crosstown Classic game at Rate Field in May. Then, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/18/cubs-sox-wrigley-field-fight" target="_blank" >a brawl in the Wrigley Field bleachers</a> garnered national attention when the teams faced off in August on the North Side.</p><p>But that type of misbehavior is nothing new.</p><p>Since the start of the 2021 season, at least 104 people have been arrested during baseball games at Chicago's two ballparks, according to Chicago police data obtained through a public records request.</p><p>Fifty-six of those arrests happened at Rate Field, compared to 48 at Wrigley Field, the data shows. Those arrested have been charged with battering fans and security guards, running onto the playing fields and repeatedly trespassing at Wrigley, among other offenses.</p><p>A Cubs spokesperson said the ballclub is “fortunate to have a strong partnership with the Chicago Police Department, whose officers work closely with our security team to provide a safe and welcoming environment for more than 3 million fans each year.”</p><p>“We do not tolerate disruptive or illegal behavior, and if an issue arises, our teams work together to address it quickly,” the spokesperson said.</p><p>A Sox spokesperson said the organization is “committed to creating a safe and enjoyable experience for every fan who visits the ballpark,” crediting the “diligent gameday staff, security personnel and law enforcement partners.”</p><h3><b>Take me out to the brawl-game</b></h3><p>Most people arrested during ballgames in Chicago have been charged with misdemeanor battery.</p><p>Back in July 2021, a 31-year-old man shoved a security guard who tried to break up a “cup snake” in the Wrigley bleachers, according to a police report. His case was dropped months later.</p><p>Later that year, a 26-year-old man hit a woman in the face after she told him to stop peeing on her car in the Rate Field parking lot ahead of an October playoff game, an arrest report shows. When others stepped in to help the woman, the man started fighting them and called for his cousin to join.</p><p>The men were charged with misdemeanor battery, according to Cook County court records. They were both sentenced to two years probation and community service.</p><p>At least 10 other fans have been arrested for running onto Rate Field in recent years, compared to four at Wrigley.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" id="image-4d0000" name="image-4d0000"></a> <picture data-crop="medium"> <source type="image/webp" width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/84a4f25/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/490x275!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/66281aa/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/980x550!/format/webp/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG 2x" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <source width="490" height="275" data-srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/daf574e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" srcset="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" /> <img class="Image" alt="Chicago Cubs' security personnel arrest a fan that ran on the field during the eighth inning of a baseball game against the Pittsburgh Pirates on Sunday, June 10, 2018, in Chicago. " srcset="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/daf574e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG 1x,https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/1931ee7/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/980x550!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG 2x" width="490" height="275" data-src="https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/dims4/default/daf574e/2147483647/strip/true/crop/3499x1964+0+447/resize/490x275!/quality/90/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fchorus-production-cst-web.s3.us-east-1.amazonaws.com%2Fbrightspot%2F31%2Fc9%2F09d720ad46bdbb707735556e2028%2Fpirates-cubs-baseball.JPG" data-lazy-load="true" src="data:image/svg+xml;base64,PHN2ZyB4bWxucz0iaHR0cDovL3d3dy53My5vcmcvMjAwMC9zdmciIHZlcnNpb249IjEuMSIgaGVpZ2h0PSIyNzVweCIgd2lkdGg9IjQ5MHB4Ij48L3N2Zz4=" > </picture> <div class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Security guards arrest a fan who ran onto Wrigley Field during a game in June 2018.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Matt Marton/AP</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>All but one were charged with felony counts of trespassing in a place of public amusement. Eight of them were found guilty or entered a plea deal, two had their charges dismissed and the other cases are ongoing, according to court records.</p><p>A 29-year-old man was arrested for running onto both Rate and Wrigley fields during games in June and September 2021, records show. At Wrigley, he held up a religious sign that said “Jesus is Lord.” And at Rate Field, he told security he jumped on the field to “repent his sins for Jesus.”</p><p>He was sentenced to 18 months of court supervision in one case, plus community service and a year of probation in the other, records show. He was also banned from attending games at professional sports stadiums during his probation.</p><p>Wrigley Field has had a bigger problem with repeat trespassers.</p><p>The list includes a 44-year-old man who was arrested at least four times in the past year and a half — despite being “forbidden” from the ballpark, records show. He was sentenced to two years conditional discharge and two years probation.</p><h3><b>Crosstown clashes </b></h3><p>A two-game Crosstown Classic series generated five arrests at Rate Field in May 2022, the most of any Cubs-Sox series in recent years. Most involved men beating up security guards after being told to leave the stadium, according to police reports.</p><p>Last month’s viral bleacher brawl at Wrigley drew a stinging rebuke from the Cubs’ Crow-Armstrong, who called the melee “unfortunate and somewhat nauseating.” The fight made headlines, but no one was charged.</p><p>A 41-year-old man was arrested that night for allegedly attacking someone as the game was wrapping up. The victim told police the man “sucker punched” him, bloodying his nose, according to a police report. The alleged instigator was charged with felony cocaine possession and misdemeanor battery. </p><p>The most serious ballpark crime in recent years has given way to an enduring mystery.</p><p>In August 2023, two women were <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2023/8/25/23846670/shooting-white-sox-game-guaranteed-rate-field" target="_blank" >struck by gunfire as they sat in the Rate Field bleachers</a> during the fourth inning of a game between the Sox and then-Oakland Athletics, according to police. A bullet was found in the hoodie of a third woman.</p><p>The White Sox have insisted the gunfire came from outside the park. Still, a 42-year-old woman who was shot in the right thigh has <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/08/26/woman-shot-white-sox-game-files-lawsuit-against-team-stadium-owners" target="_blank" >sued the team</a>, its security firm and the Illinois Sports Facility Authority, which owns and operates Rate Field.</p><p>The case is set to go to trial in January.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe width="200" height="113" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/9oAZkq9IiYs?feature=oembed" frameborder="0" allow="accelerometer; autoplay; clipboard-write; encrypted-media; gyroscope; picture-in-picture; web-share" referrerpolicy="strict-origin-when-cross-origin" allowfullscreen title="2 shot during White Sox Game at Guaranteed Rate Field, unclear if bullets came from outside stadium"></iframe> </div> </div></div><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/08/18/cubs-sox-wrigley-field-fight" target="_blank" >Man charged with sucker-punching fan at Cubs-Sox game at Wrigley Field</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2024/08/26/woman-shot-white-sox-game-files-lawsuit-against-team-stadium-owners" target="_blank" >Woman shot at White Sox game last year sues team, stadium owners</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2023/9/1/23856073/white-sox-shooting-stray-bullet-history-of-other-ballpark-shootings" target="_blank" >Stray bullet theory pushed by White Sox has 73-year history in nation’s ballparks</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: What's the worst-case scenario for a Bears team trying to avoid regression?
entries.summary: <p><i>Click </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/09/whats-the-best-case-scenario-for-the-2026-bears-as-they-try-to-top-last-seasons-wild-ride" target="_blank" ><i>here</i></a><i> for a look at the Bears' best-case scenario.</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Ben Johnson doesn’t like to talk about last season. But just three days into training camp, he let slip a popular talking point — and motivation tactic — for this year’s team.</p><p>“Well, we’re the No. 1 regression candidate,” he claimed.</p><p>No one turned the ball over less last year than the Bears. Or forced more takeaways. Or recovered a higher percentage of their own fumbles. Or had more <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/08/bears-panthers-caleb-williams-pete-crow-armstrong-kanye-west-madden-back-work-quarterback-week-1-ben-johnson-nfl" target="_blank" >fourth-quarter comebacks</a>. Those reasons — combined with the fact the Bears are going from playing a last-place schedule to a first-place one — makes this year’s challenge completely different than Johnson’s first season.</p><p>“I think we’ve got plenty of motivation,” he said.</p><p>Draw up a worst-case scenario for the Bears this season, and all those outliers return to back to normal, exposing a defensive unit that was, by many other measures, an abomination last year.</p><p>Only five teams gave up more points on drives that didn’t end with a takeaway. Only nine gave up more points, period. Those nine — the Cowboys, Jets, Bengals, Cardinals, Titans, Commanders, Giants, Raiders and Dolphins — combined to win 41 out of 152 games. None made the playoffs. More than half fired their head coach in disgust.</p><p>The Bears won the NFC North because they led the NFL with 33 takeaways. Takeaway stats typically don’t carry over from one year to the next, though. They're like bullpens — or puck luck.</p><p>In 2023, the Ravens and Giants led the NFL with 31 takeaways. The next year, the Ravens had 17 and the Giants 15.</p><p>In 2024, The Vikings and Steelers led the league with 33 apiece. The next year, the Steelers had 27 and the Vikings 21.</p><p>The one team in the last five years to defy that trend was the Cowboys, who led the NFL in takeaways in both 2021 and 2022. Their defensive backs coach during that time, Al Harris, is entering his second season with the Bears. The team is testing his ability to produce their next generation of ballhawks, though. The Bears let the NFL’s interceptions leader, safety Kevin Byard, hit free agency and join former coach Mike Vrabel in New England. Cornerback Nahshon Wright, who led all NFL players with eight takeaways last season — five interceptions and three fumble recoveries — signed with the Jets.</p><p>The Bears acknowledged their defensive shortcomings, adding speed in safeties Coby Bryant and Dillion Thieneman and linebacker Devin Bush — only to watch Bryant hurt his knee, keeping him out until at least December. Slot cornerback Kyler Gordon might not ever play for the Bears again because of a mysterious calf injury. At the least, he’ll miss the first four games.</p><p>And, oh yeah, the Bears didn’t add a relevant edge rusher.</p><p>How is the Bears defense supposed to be better?</p><p>The team’s worst-case scenario features quarterback Caleb Williams being forced to race teams to 35 to make up for a popgun defense. Johnson won’t shy away from being aggressive — It's the responsibility of the offense to score every time we hit the grass,” he said — but a pass-heavy, play-from-behind gameplan runs the risk of instilling bad habits into the young quarterback. </p><p>The watchwords for Williams’ improvement this offseason — accuracy, efficiency, getting off to a hot start — have nothing to do with playing with his hair on fire. Rather, he needs to do simple better. His completion percentage of 65% on passes 10 yards or fewer was second-worst in the NFL last year. He completed 45% of passes of 11-20 yards, the fifth-worst.</p><p>There’s nothing more important this season than Williams’ development. If the wheels come off the defense and the Bears have to spend all season chasing points, Williams’ growth will be stunted.</p><p>If that happens, the Bears are in trouble. The NFC North had the NFL’s best-ever win rate in 2024. Last year, every team had a winning record. </p><p>There’s no margin for error. Or regression.</p>
entries.author: Patrick Finley

entries.title: Illinois Dems seek DHS probe of federal agents for excessive force during Midway Blitz
entries.summary: <p>Several members of the Illinois congressional delegation are calling for the Department of Homeland Security's inspector general to formally investigate federal agents for multiple allegations of excessive use of force during last year's <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/graphics/immigration/2026/midway-blitz-by-the-numbers/" target="_blank" >Operation Midway Blitz</a>, including "accountability" for the agent who shot Chicagoan Marimar Martinez last fall.</p><p>The nine Chicago-area Democrats wrote in a letter to Joseph V. Cuffari, the DHS inspector general, that a comprehensive investigation into a severe pattern of excessive force is needed — and pointed to several findings from the Illinois Accountability Commission. The letter names 21 federal agents they say engaged in incidents of excessive force.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center><div class="Enhancement-item"> <div class="ExternalContent-wrapper" data-embed> <iframe src="https://docs.google.com/viewer?embedded=true&url=https://cst.brightspotcdn.com/73/77/3b8706a546029030b51ca5b55d2d/ramirez-letter-illinois-accountability-commission-findings.pdf"></iframe> </div> </div></div><p>The letter references Border Patrol Agent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2026/08/25/marimar-martinez-ice-border-patrol-midway-blitz-chicago-police-cpd" target="_blank" >Charles Exum</a> crashing into Martinez's vehicle and shooting her five times, with Border Patrol Agents Adam Perkins and Lorenzo Cordero also allegedly involved in the incident. Other examples include claims Border Patrol Agents Benito Nuñez, Carlos Chavira, and Jesus Guillen conducted "unauthorized high-speed pursuits" and caused crashes in residential neighborhoods after being directly ordered to stop.</p><p>And it includes reports of Border Patrol Agents Enrique Camacho, Angel Nieves, and Ricardo Moreno deploying tear gas on a road near an elementary school while children played nearby. Agents Matthew Sulek, Michael Turner, Oscar Meza, Andrew Torabpour, Joseph Brennan, Martin Davalos, Alexander Mills, Andy Chavez, Tee Rico, and Javier Puente and Timothy Donahue are also named. </p><p>The delegation is asking for internal administrative reviews or probes of incidents of excessive force involving the 21 agents. The letter also asks for steps taken by DHS to respond to reports of "escalatory or abusive behavior," consequences imposed on DHS officers "who authorized inaccurate public statements," and the status of use-of-force incidents DHS has opened for review. </p><p>After spending six months gathering testimony, video footage and legal records, the Illinois Accountability Commission <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/2026-04-iac-final-report.html" target="_blank" >put out its final report</a> in April, examining Operation Midway Blitz and the alleged abuse carried out by federal agents in and around the city. Gov. JB Pritzker assembled the commission in October to investigate federal agents’ conduct during Operation Midway Blitz. The report <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-Referral-Letter-04-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >included a letter</a> referring charges to Cook County State’s Attorney Eileen O’Neill Burke, the Chicago Police Department, the Kane County state’s attorney, and the Elgin, Franklin Park and Evanston police departments.</p><p>"There is little evidence of DHS action to investigate these incidents and hold personnel accountable," the letter reads. "We formally request you conduct investigations into these incidents and publicly determine DHS compliance with DHS policy and federal law."</p><p>The letter was signed by Sen. Dick Durbin and U.S. Reps. Delia Ramirez, Danny Davis, Mike Quigley, Bill Foster, Robin Kelly, Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, Raja Krishnamoorthi and Jonathan Jackson — and it comes a year after federal immigration agents targeted Chicago and the surrounding suburbs during Operation Midway Blitz.</p><p>"When the Illinois Accountability Commission released its findings, a DHS spokesperson attempted to dismiss the report by arguing that states lack the authority to investigate on-duty federal agents," the letter states. "While we disagree with this claim, the Office of Inspector General unquestionably possesses the public duty to investigate federal officers for misconduct, unconstitutional uses of force and potential criminal violations."</p><p>Federal agents targeted the Chicago area during Midway Blitz from mid-September through mid-October. On Sept. 12, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González,</a> a father and cook originally from Mexico, was fatally shot at “close range” as he allegedly tried to flee the U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents who tried to stop his car. Midway Blitz slowed in mid-November.</p><p>Illinois State Police opened an investigation into Villegas González's shooting in May, nearly eight months after he was killed by a federal immigration agent. </p><p>DHS in May said the shooting was “still under investigation” and insisted the agent “feared for his life” while being dragged. Tuesday's letter made no reference to Villegas González.</p><p>Martinez's shooting<b> </b>is being investigated by the Chicago Police Department's Investigative Response Team, who are looking to bring a case to Cook County prosecutors, the Chicago Sun-Times learned last month.</p>

entries.title: What's the best-case scenario for the 2026 Bears as they try to top last season's wild ride?
entries.summary: <p><i>Click </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/09/bears-worst-case-scenario-2026-season-defense-takeaways-popgun-caleb-williams-nfc-north-ben-johnson" target="_blank" ><i>here</i></a><i> for a look at the Bears' worst-case scenario.</i></p><p>Nobody painted a best-case scenario like former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> coach Matt Nagy, who said going into his fourth season the offense was on the verge of breaking through. He was so wrong about it that he gave up play-calling after three games.</p><p>When those who run Halas Hall now, mainly general manager Ryan Poles and coach Ben Johnson, present an optimistic outlook, it’s more grounded. There might be some hope that ends up appearing misplaced in hindsight, but at least it’s plausible at the time.</p><p>If things go as well as reasonably possible for the Bears, they could one-up last season and go 12-5 to take the NFC North for the second time in a row. The road to that destination would start with a convincing win at the Panthers in the season opener Sunday.</p><p>Most of their faith is in quarterback <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2025/08/31/why-do-so-many-people-hate-bears-qb-caleb-williams-he-answers-exactly-that-question" >Caleb Williams</a>, which is equal parts belief in his talent and confidence in Johnson’s ability to maximize him. It all starts there: Williams needs to be in the top quarter of NFL starters.</p><p>The fanbase might think he already is, but that’s overexuberant. He’ll get there, though, if he finds the right blend between his improvisational skills and the machinelike precision and timing Johnson is teaching.</p><p>In a review of every pass play from last season, Johnson pointed out roughly 100 of Williams’ 238 incomplete passes that he should’ve hit. Making good on even 40 of those would’ve bumped his completion percentage from 58.1 to 65.1, and at Williams’ average of 11.9 yards per completion, his yardage would’ve jumped from 231.9 (12th in the league) to 259.9 (fourth).</p><p>Potential must become production. It’s his second season under Johnson and third overall, which is typically when great quarterbacks show concrete proof of where they’re headed.</p><p>If Williams does all that, the Bears will have a chance every week. He could use a little help from a breakout season by wide receiver Rome Odunze and left tackle Ozzy Trapilo — working back from a knee injury — stepping into the starting lineup early in the season.</p><p>It's harder to buy into the defense, but maybe the Bears will be right about their pass-rushing combo of Montez Sweat and Austin Booker. Maybe defensive tackle Grady Jarrett has a resurgence in him. Maybe they found a hidden gem in sixth-round pick Jordan van den Berg at defensive tackle.</p><p>If enough of those maybes become yesses, the Bears could have a league-average defensive line, and that’d be an improvement from last season.</p><p>They’d also love to put this Kyler Gordon saga behind them.</p><p>Gordon missed most of last season with three injuries, then got hurt again in the offseason and missed all of training camp. He’ll be out at least the first four games, but if he comes back as Spiderman at nickel cornerback in Week 5, that’ll be forgotten quickly. He’s elite at his position when healthy.</p><p>And when teams use a first-round pick on a safety, as the Bears did by drafting Dillon Thieneman 25th overall, they’re expecting instant impact. The Bears are depending on that, especially after veteran safety Coby Bryant got hurt in camp, and Thieneman has looked ready at every checkpoint so far.</p><p>Bryant’s potentially season-ending knee injury was brutal and a reminder of how fortunate the Bears were last season. About half the starting lineup missed some time in camp this year, and they’ll need that to be the end of their bad luck.</p><p>Existentially, the Bears’ best-case scenario is the rest of the North enduring a worst-case scenario. It’d be awfully helpful if the Packers, Lions and Vikings remained mediocre.</p><p>That’s the equation if everything goes right this season. To whatever extent it doesn’t, the Bears’ record will slip accordingly. But the good news for them is that while that’s quite a rosy hypothetical, it’s all possible.</p>

entries.title: Bears WR Rome Odunze limited in team's first injury report
entries.summary: <p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> wide receiver <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/09/08/bears-wr-rome-odunze-day-to-day-with-injury-ben-johnson-hopeful-hell-play-in-season-opener-vs-panthers" target="_blank" >Rome Odunze</a> would have been limited in practice today because of a right calf injury had the team not had the day off.</p><p>Backup quarterback Tyson Bagent would have missed practice altogether with a back problem. He practiced Tuesday.</p><p>Left tackle Ozzy Trapilo was limited, too, as he works his way back from a patellar tendon injury. He's not expected to play in games for weeks.</p><p>Odunze walked off the field Thursday. Coach Ben Johnson said Tuesday that he considered the third-year wide receiver day-to-day and was hopeful he'd be able to face the Panthers.</p><p>Wednesday marked the first day that the NFL required the Bears to submit an injury report. The Bears did not practice Wednesday but issued an estimated report, saying what would have happened if the Bears had held practice. They'll issue injury reports again Thursday and Friday leading up to Sunday's season opener against the Panthers in Charlotte, N.C.</p>

entries.title: Jalen Brunson, NBA champion and Stevenson alum, will host 'Saturday Night Live' season premiere
entries.summary: <p>NEW YORK — Jalen Brunson, newly crowned NBA champion and former Sun-Times high school Player of the Year, will host "Saturday Night Live" when the new season begins later this month.</p><p>Brunson, who helped the New York Knicks win the title for the first time in 53 years, makes his hosting debut Sept. 26 with pop girl group Katseye the musical guest.</p><p>It will be Brunson's hosting debut on SNL.</p><p>Brunson is the fifth NBA star to be tapped as a host by the long-running late-night sketch comedy show, joining Bill Russell, Charles Barkley, Michael Jordan and LeBron James.</p><p>Brunson led Stevenson to the IHSA state championship in 2015.</p><p>Brunson averaged 28.4 points, 6.1 assists and 3.2 rebounds in 19 playoff games last season for the Knicks before leading the franchise to its first NBA title since 1973. Brunson underwent wrist surgery earlier this offseason, but is expected to return to basketball-related activities in time for the start of training camp.</p><p>The NBC sketch comedy show airs at 10:30 p.m. Chicago time and streams live on Peacock.</p><p><b>Contributing:</b> <a class="Link" href="https://www.usatoday.com/sports/" target="_blank" ><i>USA Today Sports</i></a></p>

entries.title: Open House Chicago returns for 2026 with 20 new sites to visit
entries.summary: <p>The 2026 Open House Chicago lineup, released Wednesday by the Chicago Architecture Center, brings together 20 new locations for those looking to check out some of the city's most unique buildings.</p><p>The festival, now in its 16th year and running Oct. 17-18, is "one of the largest architecture and urban festivals in the world," according to the Chicago Architecture Center. No prior registration is required, so visitors can show up as they please during open house hours and can start planning their route <a class="Link" href="https://openhousechicago.org/" target="_blank" >here</a>.</p><p>With over 200 locations across 30 Chicago neighborhoods, here's your chance to see many of the city's otherwise hard-to-see, culturally significant and historically impactful sites.</p><h3>Open House Chicago 2026 new locations</h3><ul class="ul1" id="rte-68a52f90-ac60-11f1-b6e3-d74c93e7797a"><li>Blackhawks Ice Center, Near West Side</li><li>Chicago Fire FC’s Dear Chicago Experience Center, Near North Side</li><li>Muddy Waters Mojo Museum, Kenwood</li><li>Smashed Plastic Record Pressing, Hermosa</li><li>Windy City Bird Lab, Near West Side</li><li>Sears Sunken Garden, North Lawndale</li><li>Oak Woods Cemetery, Woodlawn</li><li>Narrow Bridge Arts Club, Woodlawn </li><li>TimeLine Theatre, Uptown</li><li>Broadway in Chicago’s Cadillac Palace Theatre, Downtown</li><li>Woman’s Athletic Club, Near North Side</li><li>Chinese American Service League Kam Liu Building, Chinatown</li><li>Xchange Chicago at Gary Comer Youth Center, Woodlawn</li><li>St. Pauls United Church of Christ, Lincoln Park</li><li>Albany-Carroll Arts Building, Garfield Park</li><li>FarmZero, Downtown</li><li>Olson Kundig, Near West Side</li><li>Bronzeville Black Metropolis National Heritage Area Headquarters, Bronzeville</li><li>BandWith Chicago, Garfield Park</li><li>Griffin Museum of Science and Industry, Hyde Park</li></ul>

entries.title: Illinois service members killed in combat after 9/11 memorialized ahead of terror attack anniversary
entries.summary: <p>Anna Ware was filled with dread when she opened her door to two servicemen. </p><p>It was a week before Christmas in 2009. Her 27-year-old son Albert Ware, an Army sergeant and father of three, was serving his second tour in Afghanistan. The uniformed men on the doorstep of her Pullman home told her Albert was killed after a roadside bomb blew up his Humvee. </p><p>"I could just see death in their eyes. And I just closed the door because I didn't want to hear what they had to say," said Ware, tears streaming down her face. "I asked God to give me strength to go back and open the door." </p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item" data-crop=""> <figure class="Figure"><a class="AnchorLink" entries.title: Demócratas de Illinois piden a DHS investigar a agentes federales por uso excesivo de la fuerza
entries.summary: <p>Varios miembros de la delegación congresional de Illinois piden al inspector general del Departamento de Seguridad Nacional (DHS) que investigue formalmente a agentes federales por múltiples alegaciones de uso excesivo de la fuerza durante el Operativo Midway Blitz del año pasado, incluida la "rendición de cuentas" para el agente que disparó a la residente de Chicago, Marimar Martinez, el otoño pasado.</p><p>Los ocho demócratas del área de Chicago escribieron en una carta dirigida a Joseph V. Cuffari, el inspector general de DHS, que se necesita una investigación exhaustiva sobre un grave patrón de uso excesivo de la fuerza —y señalaron varios hallazgos de la Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois. La carta nombra a 21 agentes federales que, según ellos, participaron en incidentes de uso excesivo de la fuerza.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-8b0000" name="module-8b0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>La Voz Chicago WhatsApp</h3>Encuentra más noticias en nuestro canal de WhatsApp. <a class="Link" href="https://www.whatsapp.com/channel/0029Vb0XT1XCHDylm3rCs40P" target="_blank" ><b>Síguenos.</b></a></div> </div><p>La carta hace referencia a que el agente de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Charles Exum, embistió el vehículo de Martinez y le disparó cinco veces, y que los agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Adam Perkins y Lorenzo Cordero, también habrían estado involucrados en el incidente.</p><p>Otros ejemplos incluyen alegaciones de que los agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Benito Nuñez, Carlos Chavira y Jesus Guillen, realizaron "persecuciones a alta velocidad no autorizadas" y provocaron choques en barrios residenciales después de recibir órdenes directas de detenerse.</p><p>También incluye reportes de que los agentes de la Patrulla Fronteriza, Enrique Camacho, Angel Nieves y Ricardo Moreno, lanzaron gas lacrimógeno en una carretera cerca de una escuela primaria mientras niños jugaban en las cercanías. Se nombran también a los agentes Matthew Sulek, Michael Turner, Oscar Meza, Andrew Torabpour, Joseph Brennan, Martin Davalos, Alexander Mills, Andy Chavez, Tee Rico, Javier Puente y Timothy Donahue.</p><p>La delegación solicita revisiones administrativas internas o investigaciones sobre los incidentes de uso excesivo de la fuerza que involucran a los 21 agentes. La carta también pide información sobre las medidas que DHS tomó en respuesta a reportes de "comportamiento de escalamiento o abusivo", las sanciones impuestas a oficiales de DHS "que autorizaron declaraciones públicas inexactas" y el estado de los incidentes de uso de la fuerza que DHS ha abierto para revisión.</p><p>Tras pasar seis meses recopilando testimonios, grabaciones de video y expedientes legales, la Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/2026-04-iac-final-report.html" target="_blank" >publicó su informe final</a> en abril, examinando el Operativo Midway Blitz y el presunto abuso cometido por agentes federales dentro y alrededor de la ciudad.</p><p>El gobernador JB Pritzker formó la comisión en octubre para investigar la conducta de los agentes federales durante el Operativo Midway Blitz. El informe <a class="Link" href="https://ilac.illinois.gov/content/dam/soi/en/web/ilac/documents/final-report/IAC-Referral-Letter-04-2026.pdf" target="_blank" >incluía una carta</a> remitida a la Fiscal del Condado de Cook, Eileen O’Neill Burke; al Departamento de Policía de Chicago; a la Fiscal del Condado de Kane; y a los departamentos de policía de Elgin, Franklin Park y Evanston.</p><p>"Hay poca evidencia de que DHS haya actuado para investigar estos incidentes y responsabilizar al personal", dice la carta. "Solicitamos formalmente que usted realice investigaciones sobre estos incidentes y determine públicamente el cumplimiento del DHS con la política del DHS y la ley federal".</p><p>La carta fue firmada por el senador Dick Durbin y los representantes Delia Ramirez, Danny Davis, Mike Quigley, Robin Kelly, Jesus "Chuy" Garcia, Raja Krishnamoorthi y Jonathan Jackson —y llega un año después de que agentes federales de inmigración tuvieran como objetivo a Chicago y sus suburbios durante el Operativo Midway Blitz.</p><p>"Cuando la Comisión de Responsabilidad de Illinois publicó sus hallazgos, un portavoz de DHS intentó desestimar el informe argumentando que los estados no tienen autoridad para investigar a agentes federales en servicio", afirma la carta. "Aunque no estamos de acuerdo con esa afirmación, la Oficina del Inspector General indudablemente posee el deber público de investigar a oficiales federales por mala conducta, usos inconstitucionales de la fuerza y posibles violaciones penales”.</p><p>Los agentes federales se concentraron en el área de Chicago durante Midway Blitz desde mediados de septiembre hasta mediados de octubre. El 12 de septiembre, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2025/11/17/silverio-villegas-gonzalez-ice-dhs-trump-midway-blitz-shooting-homicide-franklin-park-chicago" target="_blank" >Silverio Villegas González</a>, un padre y cocinero originario de México, fue baleado fatalmente a "quemarropa" cuando, según se alega, intentó huir de los agentes de Inmigración y Control de Aduanas (ICE) que intentaron detener su auto. Midway Blitz se desaceleró a mediados de noviembre.</p><p>La Policía Estatal de Illinois abrió una investigación sobre el tiroteo de Villegas González en mayo, casi ocho meses después de que un agente federal de inmigración lo matara.</p><p>En mayo, DHS dijo que el tiroteo "aún estaba bajo investigación" e insistió en que el agente "temía por su vida" mientras era arrastrado. La carta del martes no hace referencia a Villegas González.</p><p>El tiroteo contra Martinez está siendo investigado por el Equipo de Respuesta Investigativa del Departamento de Policía de Chicago, que busca presentar un caso ante los fiscales del condado de Cook, informó el Chicago Sun-Times el mes pasado.</p><p><i>Traducido con una herramienta de inteligencia artificial (IA) y editado por los seres humanos de </i><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/la-voz" target="_blank" ><i>La Voz Chicago</i></a><br></p>
