entries.title: Border Protection officer accused of sex assaults became 'perfect mark' for prostitution ring, lawyer says
entries.summary: <p>The<b> </b>U.S. Customs and Border Protection<b> </b>officer<b> </b>accused<b> </b>of<b> </b><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" target="_blank" >sexually assaulting<b> </b>women</a><b> </b>in Chicago’s suburbs<b> </b>is a “flawed”<b> </b>and<b> </b>“weak”<b> </b>man<b> </b>who disgraced his family and country — but he is not guilty of robbing and raping his alleged victims, his lawyer argued Wednesday.</p><p>Rather, CBP officer Luis Uribe<b> </b>turned out to be<b> </b>“the perfect mark”<b> </b>for members of a prostitution ring overseen by a boss in China, the defense attorney insisted.</p><p>“There’s a mountain of evidence that [Uribe’s] a flawed human,” defense attorney Michael<b> </b>Clancy<b> </b>said. “But there’s no evidence of what he’s charged with.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/immigration/2025/12/09/ohare-based-border-patrol-officer-sexually-abused-robbed-women-in-2022-indictment-claims" >O’Hare-based Border Protection officer sexually abused, robbed women at gunpoint, indictment claims</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>The commentary amounted to the most full-throated defense of Uribe since a grand jury last year accused the immigration officer of sexually assaulting<b> </b>four women<b> </b>in Schaumburg<b> </b>and<b> </b>Naperville<b> </b>in 2022. It came during opening statements in Uribe’s trial, which kicked off Wednesday in the courtroom of U.S. District Judge Jorge<b> </b>Alonso.</p><p>Uribe, 45, has been held in federal custody ever since his Dec. 9, 2025, arrest.</p><p>Jurors also heard from Assistant U.S. Attorney Jonathan<b> </b>Shih. The prosecutor showed them a photo of the badge Uribe once carried, and he told the panel it<b> </b>“looks like a bald eagle sitting on top of a shield — a gold shield.”</p><p>“We are here because the defendant was not only derelict in his duty — he violated it,”<b> </b>Shih said. “Actually, he perverted it. He went from investigating crimes to committing them.”</p><p>Uribe is charged with 10 counts of deprivation of civil rights under color of law and one count of brandishing a firearm during a crime of violence. Though his indictment became public near the end of last year’s Operation Midway Blitz deportation campaign, it is not related to the Trump administration’s aggressive immigration enforcement effort.</p><p>Rather, Uribe allegedly committed six attacks between February and October 2022, while being primarily assigned to O’Hare Airport. Shih explained to jurors how, during one attack, Uribe<b> </b>“pushed his way”<b> </b>into a hotel room, “pulled out his badge with an eagle on it, and he pulled out a black handgun.”</p><p>The prosecutor described how Uribe raped the women, telling jurors one “was terrified and she was disgusted,” and another was afraid Uribe would kill her.</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago/2026/08/24/luis-uribe-customs-cbp-broadview-six" >CBP agent says feds’ ‘Broadview Six’ misconduct tainted his sexual assault case</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p>Uribe became “such a problem in the Chinese community,”<b> </b>Shih told jurors, that an effort was made to obtain a photograph of Uribe to circulate. A photo was eventually taken during a meeting at the Royal Buffet in Hoffman Estates.</p><p>Prosecutors have said the photo was taken during a meeting Uribe had<b> </b>with a sex worker, and that Uribe was offered free sex<b> </b>during the meeting<b> </b>to end the attacks.</p><p>However, Clancy told jurors it was “insulting”<b> </b>to say Uribe’s alleged victims are “part of the Chinese community.”<b> </b>Rather, he said they<b> </b>“are part of a criminal organization that runs prostitution and other crimes.”</p><p>The defense attorney said that, around 2020 and 2021, Uribe visited a prostitute who turned out to be the “on-the-ground Chicago boss of a prostitution ring that is [run] by another boss, located in China.”</p><p>Clancy said Uribe made the “fatal mistake”<b> </b>of telling that woman<b> </b>he worked for Homeland Security.</p><p>“They are hustlers,” Clancy said of the alleged victims. “They are prostitutes. They are liars.”</p>

entries.title: Amid panic over ‘pen, Cubs ‘still have all the faith’ in Jacob Webb, others to recover in time for playoffs
entries.summary: <p>MILWAUKEE – The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs/2026/09/08/jacob-webb-blows-save-chicago-cubs-milwaukee-brewers-craig-counsell-caleb-thielbar-matt-shaw-nico-hoerner-jackson-chourio-phillies-diamondbacks" >latest backbreaking homer</a> hit off closer Jacob Webb is setting off alarms across the North Side, with fans wondering how their <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/cubs" >Cubs</a> can compete in the postseason with this shaky bullpen.</p><p>If they even make it that far.</p><p>That’s probably an overreaction to back-to-back bad nights against the best team in baseball.</p><p>But as their relievers have stumbled approaching the regular season’s end, things have tightened in the NL wild-card race, and the Cubs woke up Wednesday trailing the Phillies for the top wild-card spot and only three games ahead of the third-place Diamondbacks and 3 1/2 games ahead of the next-in-line Padres.</p><p>But given they also woke up Wednesday baseball’s best offensive team and its best defensive team, there’s still plenty of reason to think their championship-level goals are attainable.</p><p>The bullpen will just have to right the ship in time. That’s a scary challenge for many in the crowd.</p><p>“Baseball’s a roller coaster,” righty reliever Trent Thornton said Wednesday. “Hardly ever do you see guys be perfect for a whole season. It ebbs and flows.</p><p>“All it is is a little blip in the grand scheme of things in the season. It’s unfortunate of the timing of everything, because obviously down the home stretch, every game matters, every pitch matters.</p><p>“But [Webb has] been fantastic all year. We still have all the faith in him and everybody else in the bullpen to get the job done.”</p><p>Webb – who brought a 24-appearance scoreless streak and a 2.21 ERA into the first of his three recent blown saves – has been fantastic for the majority of the season, unexpectedly thrust into the role of Craig Counsell’s go-to reliever with righty Daniel Palencia sidelined with injuries for much of the campaign.</p><p>“He’s a bulldog,” Thornton said of Webb. “As a reliever, you’ve got to be a goldfish. You can’t sit there and think about this, that and the other. The more negative thoughts that you let creep in your head, it doesn’t lead to good places.</p><p>“You ask any athlete, the ups and downs of being a competitor, failing for yourself and your team, it’s never easy, it’s never fun. But it’s part of the game. It’s how quickly you can learn from it and adjust and make that change, if you need it.</p><p>“But he’s a dog. Everybody in this locker room knows it, too, and he knows it.”</p><p>Webb’s not alone, though. Coming into Wednesday:</p><p>– righty trade-deadline acquisition Ryan Zeferjahn had a 6.23 ERA in his first 14 games as a Cub;</p><p>– Palencia had an 11.81 ERA in six appearances since returning from the IL;</p><p>– Thornton allowed seven runs in his last five appearances;</p><p>– lefty Ryan Rolison gave up multiple runs three different times in August;</p><p>– and lefty Caleb Thielbar had allowed 11 homers on the season.</p><p>Righty Aaron Civale has been excellent, with a 0.69 ERA in his last dozen appearances, but don’t expect a move to the ninth inning, with Counsell valuing his multi-inning ability.</p><p>As Counsell made clear after Tuesday’s loss, “the answers are not” in the minors, where notable names like righties Edward Cabrera and Shelby Miller, as well as lefty Justin Steele, are rehabbing from injuries.</p><p>Miller is perhaps the most likely to be able to make an impact, though whether he returns to form after a season-long injury layoff is as big a question mark as what the current major league bullpen can do on a nightly basis.</p><p>And so it will be about banking on the latest turn in the roller coaster being a good one. Without it, this is not a relief performance capable of getting the Cubs over a Brewers-shaped hurdle – or any other – in the postseason.</p><p>The lights have gotten bright. Can the bullpen handle the glare?</p><p>“It’s why we play the game,” Thornton said. “We play 162 games, but that last month of the season, the crowds are better, the fans are better, the intensity’s better, the games mean much more. This is fun. This is why you play the game.</p><p>“It’s OK to feel a little tension or whatever it is. It means you care. This is going to be exciting the next couple weeks.”</p>
entries.author: Vinnie Duber

entries.title: White Sox pushing back Luis Castillo for mechanical work as rotation stays in flux
entries.summary: <p>Veteran right-hander <b>Luis Castillo </b>threw a bullpen on Wednesday afternoon. Given his 7.25 ERA in a White Sox uniform and general manager <b>Chris Getz</b>’s recent comments on his delivery, it was a crucial one.</p><p>“There were some lower half mechanics that they were working on, and that seemed to be in a much better place,” Getz said of Castillo’s last start. “The upper half, the shoulder seemed to be flying open a bit more than it had in the past.”</p><p>It also was confirmation that after the Sox pushed back their rotation order on Saturday, Castillo is no longer slotted behind Wednesday’s starter <b>Davis Martin</b>. <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/white-sox/2026/09/08/sean-burke-shelled-as-white-sox-need-quick-answers-for-their-flagging-starting-rotation-will-venable-anthony-kay-zach-bove-luis-castillo-erick-fedde-davis-martin" target="_blank" ><u>Extra rest didn’t do much for </u><b><u>Sean Burke</u></b><u> on Tuesday</u></a>, but the Sox wanted a long window for tweaking Castillo’s mechanics.</p><p>Instead, Castillo will start sometime during this weekend’s series in St. Louis. <b>Erick Fedde</b>, initially the odd-man out of the rotation when Castillo arrived via trade last month, would be rested for Thursday’s finale against the Pirates, and the Sox are 17-11 when he starts or provides bulk innings. <b>Anthony Kay</b> would also be on regular rest, but as has often been the case as the Sox have patched together a group that has the fifth-highest ERA in MLB, Venable wouldn’t confirm Thursday’s starter until he knows “where we’re at at the end of today.”</p><p>With 17 games left after Wednesday, the repeated assertions that rookies <b>Noah Schultz, David Sandlin, </b>or that a rehabbing <b>Drew Thorpe</b> could be recalled for meaningful innings down the stretch are harder to figure. But that hasn’t slowed the flow of said assertions.</p><p>“There’s a number of guys down there that are going to be helpful for us at some point here,” Venable said. “A very important piece of this, getting to the end here, is having those guys available and ready to contribute.”</p><p>If Thorpe being asked to turn a lineup over twice in a division race–more than two years since he was last in the majors–feels far-fetched, multi-inning relief work is a potential fit for him and other Triple-A starters.</p><h3><b>Day off for Vargas</b></h3><p><b>Miguel Vargas</b> was out of the lineup Wednesday, as Venable aims to fit in one more breather for each of his positional regulars for the rest of the season. As is typically the case, it’s really a half-day off until a pinch-hitting opportunity arises.</p><h3><b>Roster move</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Rookie right-hander <b>Tyler Davis</b> was placed on family medical emergency/bereavement leave on Wednesday, while left-hander <b>Chris Murphy</b> was recalled. They are two of the 10 different Sox pitchers to record a save this season.</p><h3><b>Pham timeline</b></h3><h3></h3><p>Athletes are usually bullish on their recovery timelines, but there’s at least one person who thinks <b>Tommy Pham</b> will be ready to be activated from his left calf strain by Sunday.</p><p>“If you talk to Tommy, as soon as he’s eligible to come back he’s going to be ready to go,” Venable said. “We’ll see how he continues to progress over the next couple of days.”</p><h3><b>AFL-bound</b></h3><h3></h3><p>When No. 2 Sox prospect <b>Caleb Bonemer</b> reports to Glendale for the Arizona Fall League in October, he’ll have many Double-A Birmingham teammates with him. Infielders <b>Anthony DePino, Colby Shelton</b> and catcher <b>Grant Magill </b>will be the other Sox positional representatives.</p><p>After getting shut down for the season with right wrist soreness, top prospect <b>Roch Cholowsky</b> will prepare for next spring.</p>

entries.title: Chicago's plan for more Loop housing hits milestone with opening of Bellwether Residences
entries.summary: <p>City and project leaders on Wednesday celebrated the grand opening of the Bellwether Residences, the first office-to-residential building conversion to be completed under the city’s La Salle Street Corridor Revitalization program.</p><p>It marks a huge milestone for the city, whose <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/04/03/mayor-johnson-proposing-150m-tif-assistance-lasalle-street-revamp" >revitalization program</a> aims to add more housing to the Loop by redeveloping largely vacant office buildings. The program is expected to bring more than 1,000 apartments to the area, with tax increment financing assistance. </p><p>The $64.2 million Bellwether project was the first to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2025/03/27/developer-campari-r2-historic-loop-office-building-monroe-housing" >break ground in 2025</a> under the La Salle Street Corridor Revitalization program, and the developers received $28 million in TIF funds. </p><p>“That is what rebuilding Downtown looks like: taking buildings from another era and giving them new life, bringing more residents Downtown, creating affordable housing and building the kind of mixed-use neighborhood that will keep the Loop vibrant for generations to come,” Ald. Bill Conway (34th), whose ward the building falls in, said.</p><p>The Bellwether has 117 units, including 41 affordable apartments, which exceeds the program's requirement that 30% of units be affordable. That figure also represents the highest percentage of affordable units of any project in the program.</p><p>The apartments are on floors seven to 14 of the landmarked Rector Building, 79 W. Monroe St., and it welcomed its first residents the week of Aug. 31. The lower floors are home to a charter school and Walgreens.</p><p>The apartments are about 25% leased and has applications for all 41 affordable units, according to Gary Stoltz, principal and chief design and development officer for Chicago-based R2 Companies.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="Enhancement-item"> <bsp-carousel class="Carousel Enhancement" and two-bedroom options, with amenities such as in-unit washer and dryer and quartz countertops. There's also a lounge, fitness center with saunas, roof deck and dog run.</p><p>For all the modern finishes, there’s numerous historical elements that were kept by R2 and Lagfin S.C.A., which led the project. Lagfin S.C.A. is the holding company of Italian spirits company <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/the-watchdogs/2024/05/24/carmen-rossi-brandon-johnson-lori-lightfoot-lobbying-brown-derby-luca-garavoglia-campari" target="_blank" ><u>Campari Group</u></a>. A limited liability corporation tied to Campari Group purchased the building for an estimated $48 million in 2022.</p><p>The open staircases on each floor are original to the 1905 building, Stoltz said. And each unit's entry door, featuring smooth wood and fluted glass, are original, though R2 had to make about 50 new doors because the number of units outnumbered the property's office suites.</p><p>The developers also restored the building’s <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/07/14/iconic-loop-weather-bell-rector-bell-federal-savings-loan-shine-again-years-dark" >iconic weather bell, </a>as required by the state’s historic preservation division. The bell now bears the word “<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/architecture-design/2026/08/13/photos-loop-iconic-weather-bell-federal-savings-building-back-action" >Bellwether</a>,” in reference to the apartment building.</p><p>The Rector Building — formerly known as the Bell Federal Savings & Loan Building — was built in 1905. It’s the oldest surviving commercial tower designed by architect Jarvis Hunt and was given landmark status by the Chicago City Council on March 12, 2025.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>Giacomo Zanibelli, director of real estate at Lagfin S.C.A., shakes hands with Mayor Brandon Johnson during the grand opening of the Bellwether Residences in the Loop.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Pat Nabong/Sun-Times</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>“When we began this project, we shared a vision: To imagine an important Chicago landmark in a way that honored its history while meeting the needs of the city today,” Giacomo Zanibelli, director of real estate at Lagfin S.C.A, said. “Today, its historic character has been preserved, while the building has been given new importance and a new life.”</p><p>Department of Planning and Development Commissioner Ciere Boatright said the goal of the city's La Salle program is to create mixed-use vitality and mixed-income diversity, both of which are essential for sustainable growth.</p><p>The program's six projects — which includes properties shortlisted under former Mayor Lori Lightfoot's La Salle Street Reimagined initiative — will increase Downtown's affordable housing stock by 1,000%, according to Chicago Department of Housing Commissioner Lissette Castañeda.</p><p>Boatright said when the DPD and the Department of Housing launched the La Salle initiative in 2022, the amount of vacant office space in Downtown was equal to six Willis Towers, and investors were shy to bet on Downtown because of the lagging office rebound.</p><p>Downtown's office vacancy now hovers around 24.4%, according to a July report from commercial real estate firm Colliers. The report also found growing demand for trophy office spaces — those that are newer with high-quality amenities, unlike many of the LaSalle Street buildings that are now being converted.</p><p>The private-public partnership of the La Salle initiative is also drawing more private investment. Three more city-led office-to-residential conversion projects are underway, in addition to roughly two dozen private conversions, Mayor Brandon Johnson said. Once complete, those private projects will create more than 4,000 homes in Downtown.</p><p>The conversions will create “a dynamic future” while also honoring Chicago's history, Johnson said.</p><p>“Through the Build Better Together initiative, our equitable economic development plan, we will continue to utilize our $1.25 billion housing and economic development bond, the largest public investment in housing in the city's history, as well as our partnerships to revitalize and strengthen our neighborhoods,” Johnson said. “We will also continue to think boldly, just as we have done here with the Bellwether residences, to make sure that all of our residents and families can put down roots that span generations in any neighborhood in Chicago.”</p>

entries.title: Sky’s Kate Martin is still figuring out who she is as a player
entries.summary: <p>What stands out about the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" >Sky’s</a> newest player, Kate Martin, beyond her freckles and Illinois roots, is her positive attitude.</p><p>That may sound like something used to describe a player without any real basketball chops, but Martin does have chops.</p><p>Drafted No. 18 by the Aces in 2024, she surprised many who thought she was just a college sidekick to megastar Caitlin Clark. She shot 35.5% from three-point range as a rookie on a top-notch Aces squad, then played a meaningful bench role for the expansion Valkyries.</p><p>Still, that positive attitude — her ability to reframe difficulty as opportunity — has served Martin well in the early part of her career. After a promising first two seasons, she was cut by the Valkyries at the beginning of this one.</p><p>Then the Sparks took a flier on her, first on a development contract and later on a standard one, but she never really cracked the rotation.</p><p>She was waived at the end of August and is now on her fourth team in three years.</p><p>Cue Martin’s gift for finding the silver lining.</p><p>“You can look at it one of two ways,” Martin, 26, said of her trajectory so far. “I crave stability. I would love to find my home and my niche. But also, I’ve learned so many great things from so many people. I’ve made so many friendships. I’ve learned different systems. I’ve learned how coaches operate. I learned what’s good in practice, what might not work in practice.”</p><p>So what appealed to Martin about the Sky, who are 15-25 and offered her a development contract for the final morsel of the season?</p><p>“Beggars can’t be choosers,” she said with a smile. “I’m very grateful that I even got a call. I honestly thought my season was probably going to be over with only four games being left. ... My goal is to make an impact and make the most of the next couple weeks.”</p><p>Martin’s honesty and authenticity have helped her form strong relationships everywhere she has played. So it was no surprise when she named half the Sky’s roster as already-made friends from Unrivaled, or when she mentioned her desire to coach someday.</p><p>But as a player, at this moment, she feels like she is still figuring out who she is.</p><p>“Each team I’ve played, you play different roles,” she said. “I’m gonna figure out what my role is here and then just be myself. Just like always, give it my all, do my best, make the right reads, play hard.”</p><p>In Chicago, she’ll have a longtime believer on her side: Tyler Marsh, who was an Aces assistant during Martin’s rookie season. He texted her when the Valkyries released her, telling her, “If I ever have the opportunity to get you, I’m gonna take advantage of it.”</p><p>In Martin, he sees the kind of versatility that has been typical of the Sky’s roster this year. He thinks she has been pigeonholed as a three-point shooter at the pro level, but sees potential in her as a driver and finisher.</p><p>He also thinks she has gotten quicker, which will help her on the perimeter and defensively.</p><p>As he often does with young players, Marsh emphasized the need for patience and grace with Martin.</p><p>But her toughness and selflessness are the traits he most wants the team to embody.</p><p>“Ty isn’t just about basketball and on-court skills,” Martin said. “He’s a people person. I think I can bring a lot of value to a team other than just basketball. Ty sees that. I think we align in the culture pieces.”</p><p>Martin still needs to, as she put it, find her niche on the court. But her attitude is part of why she keeps earning chances to do so.</p>

entries.title: Bally's Council committee hearing turns into a political 'circus' with more questions than answers
entries.summary: <p>Bally’s said Wednesday it has the financing to deliver a $1.7 billion casino and entertainment complex in River West, but <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/city-hall/2026/08/12/ballys-permanent-casino-river-west-construction-slowdown-council-members-letter" >slowed construction</a> of “non-gaming elements” of the project to protest video gambling terminals with potential to “cannibalize” casino revenue.</p><p>An executive team representing the gambling giant told the City Council’s License Committee that it would be “irresponsible to go forward” with all of the promised bells and whistles without knowing how much gambling competition Bally's would ultimately face.</p><p>The decision to lay off 136 employees and halt construction of roughly 12% of the project was portrayed as a re-set — and not a violation of Bally's host agreement with the city.</p><p> Bally’s made its $4 million annual lump-sum payment to the city on Tuesday as a sign of its commitment to honor the agreement.</p><p>The Illinois Gaming Board has approved 65 applications for Chicago video gambling terminals. But Bally's President and Interim Chief Financial Officer George Papanier said company officials have "no idea where that number would end up."</p><p>“That could, in effect, be adding several casinos within the marketplace where we thought we had a form of exclusivity in," Papanier said. "As a result of that, we’re re-evaluating everything outside of the HCA agreement to determine whether it’s fiscally responsible for us as a company to continue to invest at that level without the type of return that we would expect.”</p><p>The $1.7 billion casino project has encountered financial and logistical challenges since Bally’s was <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2022/5/25/23141244/ballys-casino-approved-chicago-city-council-river-west-medinah-temple-lightfoot-police-fire-pensions" target="_blank" >selected</a> to build Chicago’s casino in 2022, including an <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/casinos-gambling/2024/03/12/ballys-chicago-casino-buyout-soo-kim" target="_blank" >$800 million</a> “funding gap,” <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/2024/1/22/24047289/ballys-casino-hotel-tower-plans-changes-city-hall-chicago-river" target="_blank" >changes to its hotel plans</a> and delays that pushed the permanent casino’s expected opening into 2027.</p><p>But the revised deadline will be honored, Papanier said.</p><p>“We are going to deliver the event center, 100 rooms of the hotel and the required food and beverage components,” Papanier said.</p><p>“The components that are being reset and re-contemplated are being considered all in conjunction with the proliferation of VGTs… There’s anywhere from a 30 to a 50% impact on top line revenue… It would be irresponsible for us to trudge forward with components that are not required until we understand what the landscape looks like.”</p><p>Downtown Ald. Brendan Reilly (42nd) has long opposed the selection of Bally’s and the decision to build the casino complex in River West. He condemned what he called now-former Mayor Lori Lightfoot’s eleventh-hour “switcheroo” that designated Medinah Temple as the site for Bally’s temporary casino.</p><p>Like a prosecutor, Reilly asked Papanier whether Bally’s was slowing construction because it "lacks confidence in the Chicago market or because it lacks confidence in its ability to finance the entire project."</p><p>“The answer to that is neither," Papanier said. "Our concern around the cannibalization of VGTs and what they can do... what they’ve proven to do across the state, is the true concern here and why we’re actually discussing a reset as opposed to delivering or over-delivering every component and then some that was required” by the host agreement.</p><p>Reilly didn't buy it. Reading from a recent earnings call, Reilly quoted Bally’s own lender as saying that potential competition from video gambling terminals in Chicago was already factored into the gambling giant’s earning assumptions.</p><p>“We all know that you were struggling to cobble together money. You have an incredible debt load and you’re trying to blame all of this on…VGTs — where not a single machine is lawfully operating today yet there are thousands of [illegal] sweepstakes machines doing that,” Reilly said.</p><p>Reilly unleashed most of his anger at Mayor Brandon Johnson’s top aides: senior mayoral adviser Jason Lee and chief of staff Cristina Pacione-Zayas. </p><p>They were invited to Wednesday’s hearing, but chose not to appear. Instead, they sent Johnson's chief financial officer, who’s been on the job for a few weeks.</p><p>“Hooray for public transparency. If I’m a taxpayer in the city of Chicago, I’m disgusted,” Reilly said. “The mayor is not doing his job enforcing the [host agreement]. They’re allowing folks to play games with union jobs, people's livelihoods and honestly, our police and fire pensions — which require this casino to be incredibly successful.”</p><p>Ald. Marty Quinn (13th) sounded exasperated. “This is a circus. Congratulations Bally’s for being part of a circus,” Quinn said.</p><p>License Committee Chair Debra Silverstein (50th) closed the three and a half hour hearing with a promise to meet again — this time with Lee and Pacione-Zayas on the political hot seat.</p><p>"It's very disappointing, very embarrassing, very insulting — any adjective you can think of — that we don't have representation from the mayor's office here today to answer our questions," Silverstein said. </p>
entries.author: Fran Spielman

entries.title: Man critically wounded Humboldt Park shooting
entries.summary: <p>A man was critically injured during a shooting in Humboldt Park Wednesday afternoon, according to Chicago police.</p><p>The man, 32, was in the 700 block of North Ridgeway Avenue at 2:29 p.m. when two people approached him and fired shots, police said. The man was shot in the chest and taken to Mt. Sinai Hospital in critical condition.</p><p>No one is currently in custody, police said. </p>
